content:
I don't think cold email is dying as much as everyone says. Granted, the conversion rate on all marketing channels trends towards zero.

Here's my case study.

We get 80 positive responses per day for our PR customer, Pathos. 

We look at the prospect's website and pick the publication they should be in. TechCrunch, the Wall Street Journal, Entrepreneur.

"Do you want to get featured in this? If we wrote an article for you, it would be about [topic]."

AI writes the publication pick and the article angle for every contact.

So why does this work when something like "bookkeeping services" doesn't?

Buyers have more access to education than ever. They can ask ChatGPT about anything. Email a founder about bookkeeping and they've heard it a hundred times. They know this offer exists and where to get it when they need it. 

Offshore staffing also has had a similar spike in easy to acquire customers and then fallen off in the past years because it's so easy. Remember how crazy it was to hire someone near shore or offshore the first time you did it? 

But not every founder knows you can just pay writers to help you to get into major publications.

Outbound works better when you're showing people offers that they didn't know existed.

I replaced my entire agent setup in about an hour last month, and the only reason it was an hour is a file I made months before I needed it.

Months ago I told Claude Code and Codex to go update a GitHub repo describing who I am and what this business does. Not a README for a codebase. Context. What we sell, how we run campaigns, what our SOPs are, the skills we already had written.

At the time it felt like housekeeping. It turned out to be the thing that made me portable.

When I set up a new agent, the whole onboarding was pointing it at that repo and then one prompt: after you look at my GitHub, make a list of all the tools you are going to need API keys for so I can onboard you.

It came back with Smartlead, OpenAI, Prospeo, Blitz, MillionVerifier, Fathom and the rest of it. So instead of me trying to remember the twenty places my business actually lives, it handed me the checklist and we went down it one at a time.

Then I asked what bots it thought we should have, and it built them.

The lesson I would take from this is not about which tool I moved to. It is that your company context should not live inside any one vendor's memory. The day you want to try something else, everything you know has to be a folder you can point at.

If you have not got that repo, that is the thing to do this week. Ask your coding agent to write down who you are and what you do, and keep it somewhere you own.

For challenging me and sharing your journey.

And most of all, for being a friend.

content:
If you’ve never run a cold email campaign, listening to this list building rule is going to increase your reply rates by at least 2x and in some cases more. 

Early this year, I set on a mission to create an AI agent that could look at a website and generate a cold email campaign with no human in the loop that got leads. 

It was way way harder to build than I thought. 

One thing that we learned was that any campaign we launched needed to have at least 8 search filters (or the most you could have while retaining 3,000 contacts in the list) in order for an agent to be successful. 

When we audited why things weren’t working, the messaging was generally correct but missing some punch when we looked contact by contact. 

Many of the lists AI was creating were just ok and what most people think to make. 

Employee headcount, job title, location, industry filters. Some company keywords here and there. 

We then said we need to make these lists way tighter and gave all of the filters you can use in a Clay search (at the bottom of the post for you to give your Agent). 

This honestly was the silver bullet that cracked our efforts for an Agent to get leads without any human in the loop. The messaging was so much tighter and it spoke to their needs / problems in the AI generated copy. 

So if you’ve never launched your own campaign, I’d highly recommend this as a mental model so you stop spraying and praying. 

Filters you can search for out of the box in Clay and we have unlimited search!

- Industry

- Company size band

- Exact employee count

- Social follower count

- Year founded

- Company type

- Annual revenue range

- Employee growth over 3, 6, 12 and 24 months

- B2B vs. B2C business model

- Clay's AI industry classification

- AI sub-industry (e.g. AI and ML platforms, cloud infrastructure software)

- Revenue stream (SaaS, subscriptions, services, transaction fees, etc.)

- Products and services, matched by meaning rather than keywords

- NAICS codes

- Parent company vs. subsidiary

- Keywords in the company description

- Specific domains to include or exclude

- Location: country, state, city, ZIP, region, HQ or any office

- Tech stack: vendor, product and category

- Job postings: title, description keywords, seniority, employment type, location, date posted, still open, recruiter

- People at the company: how many current employees match a title, seniority or location (e.g. 3+ people in sales)

content:
My favorite ways to find emails no one else is emailing that gets us a 3.2x increase in replies.

In order to find the emails no one else is emailing, you have to understand how most emails are found.

It might come as no shock that most of your emails can be guessed. Everyone has some variation of their name at their domain.

That’s how most emails are found. Catch all domains and some other things throw a wrench in that which we don’t have time to get into here. But here’s some ways you can get around it.

1. Use tools like Exa/Claygent/Parallel/Context.dev to search for their email on the open web. You can try doing it with google search scrapers like OpenWebNinja but since you don’t know the email you’re searching for, it gets a bit tough.
2. Search the website by crawling it with Zenrows and regex. While you’re at it, if you don’t find a contact’s email address but you find their colleague, you can try that permutation pattern instead.
3. Verify their LinkedIn still says they work at the company and if the Clay waterfall says an email isn’t valid because it’s catchall, try that email in the haveIbeenpwned API. It’s a database of emails that have been in data leaks intended for people to know if their info has been leaked. But if their email is in there and they still work at the company, it’s a roll of the dice but I’m willing to email it.
4. For smaller companies, emailing the generic info@ email and naming the contact works really well and most people are sleeping on this.

Then custom scraping directories, google maps, government databases, discolike/ocean https databases to find websites not in traditional databases can do more of the heavy lifting on finding more companies.

Once you have the company, you can follow similar approaches above to find the contacts/ emails. Those are where the real gold is but less scalable for a lot of people.

content:
A campaign with a low reply rate and a campaign whose reply rate fell off a cliff are two different problems, and here's how we tell them apart before touching the copy.

We pull reply rate per domain and per inbox on a 7 day and a 14 day window. That part is normal.

The part I would add for you is a separate alarm that fires on the size of the drop, not the level.

An inbox that was at a 1.5% reply rate and comes back at 0.2% gets looked at that day. It is still technically sending. Nothing in the dashboard is red.

Because a rate that was always bad is a list problem or an offer problem. A rate that was fine last week and is dead this week is almost always mechanical, and there are two things I check.

First, did we email a spam trap. If a trap address got into the list in the last day, those domains need to come out immediately, they are going to get tanked either way. This is worth moving to a more premium validation provider over, one that actually screens for traps. I always forget which ones do it, so ask around before you buy.

Second, content fingerprinting. Same text going out enough times that Google recognizes it.

Small thing on that second one. If you ask Claude to spintax an email, it will often just swap one word per sentence and call it done. Tell it you want word level spintax and you get real variation, and check that your signature and your unsubscribe language got spintaxed too, because most people only do the body.

Ask Claude or Codex to build the alarm against your sending tool's API. Mine is a scheduled job that just tells me which inboxes moved the most since last week.

content:
Grok Bot built my website visitor to outbound workflow end to end. The site tags, the webhooks, the Slack alerts and the Clay tables, with zero human intervention.

At AirOps this took me a week. I downloaded all the data from GSC, RB2B and HubSpot, dug through it by hand to see which pages people actually visited and which ones converted, top and bottom of funnel. AirOps had thousands of pages to stack rank. Then I built every Clay table myself.

Between Clays MCP and browser use, Grokbot built all of it for me. Our site is maybe 75 pages, so there was way less to stack rank. I just described what I wanted.

Sending is the easy part. Anyone can blast every visitor the same message. The real move is personalizing on who they are and what they looked at, without ever saying "saw you on our site." Nobody wants that email.

How it works:

1. Clay Web Intent for company-level, Squid for person-level. 
2. Visitors flow into Clay for classification, copy creation and upserting into Bison
3. Filter before you enrich. No agencies, competitors, gov, schools, customers or your own team.
4. AI picks up to 3 real buyers at each company, deduped on LinkedIn if its company level identification.
5. An email waterfall finds and validates every address. Every lead needs a first name, last name, LinkedIn and a valid email.
6. Every piece of content is tagged by role and industry so AI can match it to the person.
7. Each key page gets its own campaign and angle.
8. A lint check blocks any email that hints at a visit, links outside our library or breaks our style rules.
9. Every visitor posts to Slack with pages viewed, time on site and the contacts found, so the team sees every visitor in real time.

Company-level visitors get a low friction, value additive email with a soft CTA. AI writes one line on what the company sells, then email 2 sends a piece of Apero content picked for their role. Sales leaders get outbound pieces, ops gets CRM, founders and investors get PE or VC pieces.

Person-level visitors get page-specific copy. Pricing, case studies, blog, contact page with no submit and repeat visitors each have their own campaign. Pricing visitors get "was your team sizing up what working with us would look like?" Sort of similar to "you forgot something in your cart" ecomm emails. 

Tools: Clay, Squid, LeadMagic, EmailBison, Salesforce, Slack, GitHub, Cursor, Vercel.

Write the spec first. The end state, the non-negotiables, and what done looks like. With AI you should spend more time scoping and developing guardrails on your desired finished state than you should actually building anything. 

If you want the exact Grok Bot prompt I used, DM me and I'll send it over.

If you want to test it - visit our site on monday when the system goes live :)

content:
My real benchmark for how smart a model is: does it finish the work. Here's the loop I run it on every day.

Every day I round up everything that has to get done and all of it goes into ClickUp. Then I open each task and dictate the plan straight into it with Wispr Flow. It is the exact same planning prompt I would write if I were about to sit down and do that task myself.

Then I say one thing. Read all the open tasks in ClickUp, they all have plans inside them, write one gigantic plan with finish conditions on every part of it, hand them out to sub agents, and go do the work. Ask me any clarifying questions you need.

That is my whole day. It is my favorite thing to do with AI and I wish it was easier to show you.

With Opus 4.8 and the models before it, we would get 90% of the way there and the last 10% was a grueling battle every single time.

Fable 5 was the first model that got everything across the line. It listened to the run conditions and the finish conditions the best and it needed the least oversight from me of anything I have run.

Then I looked at my usage. One day of this and Fable had burned 85% of my account and I had to move over to Codex.

I ran the same work on Opus 5 this week. All of it finished, on 8% of my usage.

That is my own run on my own tasks, so take it as one data point and not a benchmark.

The reason the plan lives in ClickUp and not in a chat window is that the task is already where I write down what done looks like. The model gets the goal and the finish condition in the same place every time, and I never re-explain it.

content:
People ask me every week whether Prospeo has the best coverage. or Clay, or Blitz etc etc.  Here's how to answer that for your own niche instead of taking my word for it.

The honest answer first: I buy all of them mostly for rate limit purposes. As long as the pricing works out I don't really care, I stay subscribed because the coverage is different and I would rather have it sitting there. If you can't afford all of them, my opinion on what has good coverage is not useful to you.

So run the test.

Every one of those providers is built on LinkedIn data. Sales Navigator is the most up to date copy of it. So Sales Nav is your answer key.

Build a Sales Navigator search for your exact niche. AI already knows how those links are constructed, so you can just ask for one. CEOs, 11 to 50 employees, marketing services, United States. It'll spit out the URL. Check that it actually loads and have Claude keep fixing it if it doesn't.

No Sales Nav license? On Apify there's the Harvest API and it'll scrape Sales Navigator for you. Right now that's $0.004 per lookup.

Then pull the same list out of every provider you're considering, with their API or a browser automation, and see who gets closest to the Sales Nav list.

That's your answer. Not mine. And it might be different next quarter, and it will definitely be different for a different niche.

I see people subscribed to five different data products who have never checked whether three of them already cover the same 90% of what they need.

Run the test before you buy something you don't need.

After we help teams do a bulk CRM clean up, we help them build CRMs that clean themselves.

Here's the blueprint we run.

⠀
1. Audit
⠀
Step one. We export a snapshot and measure fill rates on every field that matters: title, LinkedIn, country, email validity, segment.
⠀
2. Create individual segments we'll be working on
⠀
Every messy CRM breaks the usual six ways:
Duplicates. Contacts at a company that already has an account. Job changers. Bounced emails. Missing fields. Leads with no account.
⠀
Each one gets its own rule.
⠀
3. Approve before anything writes
⠀
We always do a backup export first. Then work with our client through each list view.
⠀
4. Enrich with a waterfall
⠀
Clay helps us set up the entire workflow (no pun intended but we do use clay's CLI to help build these), for the right enrichment, and routing.
⠀
We then have bad emails get replaced. Job changers are tracked properly, and previously empty properties are now filled.
⠀
5. Keep it on
⠀
New inbound leads, records reps add by hand, job-change signals all run through the same pipeline we put together.
⠀
That's the difference between a cleanup project and a clean CRM.

Do you have evergreen flows in place to clean your CRM?

Take this as your sign that tracking open rates is not worth it. Same copy, same lead filters, same day. 4.8% reply  vs .8% reply rate. 

 Yes, the open rate is tremendously high (artificially by robots) but you can't get this open rate without your inboxes getting great delivery. 

Despite such great delivery, the reply rate is almost 5x worse. 

Why? When you track opens, google and microsoft show these warnings in the inbox saying "Images in this message are hidden. Mark as spam?" 

If you literally google this, you'll see what I mean. 

So even though we get great delivery on these inboxes (100% google zapmail by the way), adding the open tracking kills the reply rate because of that warning in the inbox. 

We have recently had customers ask us to just test it a little bit and I'm even going to book mark this for myself to show them because I've never seen the difference to be so stark. 

The only reason we even caught this is because the open tracking was accidentally left on, leaving a natural experiment for us to view.

Most new in role lists are wrong in the same way, and the fix is one column.

When you pull people who started a role in the last few months, you get two completely different humans in the same file.

Somebody who just walked into a new company. And somebody who has been there four years and got a title bump.

You cannot send them the same email. The new hire has not picked any vendors yet. The promoted person picked all of them already.

So we do not trust a start date on its own.

We find the person, pull their entire LinkedIn profile with the Clay integration, and then read the current experience. End date empty, start date 2026-05 for example. 

Then a formula checks whether that is actually a new hire or a promotion, so the email says the appropriate thing.

That one column decides the whole message.

content:
Just gave a talk about how to turn Codex/OpenClaw/Hermes (whatever you'd like) into a real employee for your business in 3 steps. Here it is for those that couldn't be at the event. 

I fully believe that these models are incredibly intelligent now and their tool calling has gotten so good. If you aren't using AI as an employee in your business, you just haven't put the energy in to get it done. 

Everyone can get started in 3 steps. The first 2 you should drop what you're doing this Friday afternoon and get them done right away. The last step takes more time. 

The agents need context, connections, and practice creating in order to be useful. 

1. Tips to gather context

For most of us, our world is recorded digitally and written down in Slack and CRM systems. 

Give these tools access to whatever you're comfortable with and have it start building a company brain for yourself from the transcripts of your calls, the conversations in your Slack, and your email. 

Whatever you can give it go for it. 

Someone asked me yesterday how I keep the context organized. The truth is beyond just asking Claude to organize itself I don't think about this at all. 

With a million-token context window, that's as much text as the Bible. My business for sure isn't that complicated. 

Have it create a local brain in markdown files. Use Obsidian (which is free) if you want to get fancy.

2. Give the agents connection to tools

This is going to sound like the dumbest suggestion but it was really a blocker for my team to get the API keys that were necessary in order to make the most use of these agents. 

It felt like "we have too many tools, I wish I just had a list of everythign so I could get it done in 10 minutes."

Your search history on your browser has everything.

Grab the last 30 days of the sites you visit and dedupe them in a google sheet. 

Pick out the ones you want to give access to your agents and you're done. 

3. Build a loop so it can actually work for you. 

After we built this, it feels so obvious but I think this is the number one tip to get people to start using AI. 

Tell your agent to run a scheduled task any time new work is created 

A client call
An internal call
check slack every 30 minutes

Wherever a record of work is created. 

 Use the schedule task for it to read the task. Based on the context that you gave it in your company brain and what it has done for you in the past, try to suggest the plan for how the agent would execute this for you. 

Edit and accept as necessary so the agent can start doing real work. 

 This proactive loop, where a suggestion for work that the agent can take on so that you can get a message every day in Slack after a meeting or something, is the thing that really increased the rate of learning for our agent. 

Instead of us coming up with ideas of how the agent could help us, the agent was doing the work for us. It has been absolutely pivotal in making this work.

content:
I think the best cold email campaigns have 3 things in common. A campaign that drives ROI doesn't need all 3, but each one of these points drives significantly more replies. 

Ever since we started doing free tests for companies to work with us, we've launched quite possibly 3-5x more campaigns with different offers than we previously would. 

Before, I thought I could tell from one look if a campaign was going to work, now, I'm basically never surprised. I've tried to put my finger on what makes a great campaign versus others and this is what I've been thinking. 

1. Great campaigns communicate the promise to either help companies make more money, save 90% of time, save 90% of costs in a way that the recipient didn't know about with a next step that is easy to say yes to. 

The best type of offer to convert cold traffic is an offer that helps people make more money for sure. If you can, always lead with that. 

If you can't, the time savings / cost savings you can provide has to be orders of magnitude higher. 

When Instantly.ai first released a sequencer with unlimited inboxes where everyone else was charging per mailbox, the community went crazy. And that was maybe a 99% cost reduction depending on your scale. 

Save Time/Save Money offers have to be orders of magnitude better than what they are doing today. 

2. Great campaigns communicate a mechanism that the recipient didn't know existed. 

I think the increase in amount of outbound messages people are receiving is maybe responsible for 20% in the decrease in outbound effectiveness. (I'll make another post demonstrating this). 

The bigger driver of the decrease in outbound effectiveness is that prospects have access to more information than ever before. 

They know that performance outbound lead gen, bookkeeping, HR management, payroll automation, cyber security, recruiting, are all things they can get access to. And when they're ready they will find you. 

They don't know that 

- Trigify.io can find customers talking about their exact problem

- That negative google reviews can be removed with a proper appeal process 

- That Forbes is more pay to play than you might think

- That the Donut can target newsletter subscribers by income/interest

- That Starbridge can get them a list of governments that have open RFPs. 

So the second thing great outbound campaigns do is present a mechanism they didn't know was possible. 

3. The best outbound campaigns explain the value in taking the next step AND the next step is easy. 

It costs Young Dental $200-$300 to get a dentist to request a sample through Facebook ads. 

With us, it costs ~$40. 

Their campaigns if anything are a time saving / reducing risk of a bad patient experience type offer. Not make more money. And these dentists don't know that these products exist. 

But the call to action being to get a free sample set sent to their office is such a no brainer that they get tons of responses.

content:
The age of your domain when you start sending is a lever almost nobody pulls.

Here is the normal way it goes. You want to start outreach. You buy domains. You warm them for two weeks. You start sending on a domain that is two weeks old.

Normal tried and true. 

We have now seen a lot of success buying the domains we need to start sending in 2 weeks and then buying more and just sitting on them. 

We have to pay the one time domain cost but we don't put inboxes on them, we just let them sit. 

Then, when we need the domains because the others have started to lose their reply rate effectiveness, we use these domains that have aged for 3 or 4 months instead of completely fresh ones. 

Still needs warmup. You can rush a 1 week warmup but we try to do 2 weeks still. 

Those domains perform better. Consistently enough that we changed how we buy.

If you are doing consistent cold outreach, buy some domains you know are going to sit around for a bit and see if they perform better than 2 week old domains when you need them!

content:
People keep telling me they don't get what makes Audiences in Clay different from a regular contact sourcing platform. It solves 3 main problems. 

You can think of Audiences as an always on list that updates as contact information changes that can be filtered on tons of data points out of the box you don't need to build yourself. 

Problem 1: When you pull contacts from other tools, they go stale and you need to update them. Usually, paying for credits along the way to update everything. 

With Audiences, everything that qualifies for your search filters is updated automatically by contact, company, and open jobs filters. And then you can niche down into the full list with Segments to launch micro campaigns. You should read brendan short's piece on micro campaigns. 

Problem 2: Many (not all, Prospeo does a great job of this too) tools are basically copies of what you can get from public company social profiles and they let you filter on that. 

Derived data points (which I'll put at the bottom of this post) let's you not only filter on regular filters, but custom filters made by the Clay team. 

You can then get all these data points to be able to feed into your AI tools for personalization, qualification, etc. 

Problem 3: Even if you are getting the data updated, you have to connect the new data to your custom enrichments. When workflows goes live for everyone, you'll be able to automatically enrich every new company or contact immediately as they're found and push them to campaigns automatically that fit your segmentation. 

Really, my favorite part of Audiences is that everything is updated automatically so you can keep the filters and not have to think about updating it.

content:
For one of our customers we're getting 80 to 100 positive responses a day and I don't touch the account. A Grok bot does four jobs on a cron.

Here's what has to stay true every day or a campaign like this dies.

1. Enough leads in the campaign.

Every day Grok Bot checks how many leads are not started. If it's ever under 100,000 it pulls from our Supabase, which tracks who we emailed in the last 60 days, who we re-reached in the last 30, and what month we last touched them, so nobody gets hit more than once a quarter. Then it fires them at a Clay webhook and the Clay CLI workflow does the cleanup, the enrichment, and the AI content.

2. Volume actually going out.

At noon it checks how many emails went out that day. If something locked up and we're under-sending, it rechecks the campaigns and refills them itself.

3. Daily Deliverability check

It reads our inbox table in Supabase every morning. If a domain was replying at 1.5% and drops to 0.2% day over day, it pulls that domain out, cancels the subscription, and swaps another one in.

4. The Friday inbox destroyer

Every Friday it looks for domains that have sent over 200 emails with under a 0.7% reply rate overall. Those get scheduled for cancellation and pulled out of the campaigns. Then it tells me how many domains we need to buy to replace them. I audit that, make the correction, and put the order in at Hypertide.

The reason it's Grok Bot and not the other agent harnesses is boring. The cron job actually fires. I have set one up in Hermes, then checked in three times wondering why it never ran. 

Codex or Claude schedules can totally do this too but if my computer is off it won't run.

content:
Every B2B offer in the world is one of four things. Make money, save money, save time, or reduce risk.

We used to give all four equal weight and run experiments across them. After a year of running AI on every campaign, we mostly only use one of them now.

Make more money.

I think the reason is simple. If somebody believed they could save money by doing a thing, they would have already done it. Saving is a problem people have made peace with. New revenue is not.

Saving time/money are the runners up and it works. But nowhere near as well as helping people make more money.

I talked to a founder last week with an AI that spins up ad campaigns. His pitch was that you could test 10 creatives a day without a team. All time saving offerings. He got zero positive responses.

So I asked him how long it actually takes his product to find a winning ad. He said on average 21 days to crack a client's top three.

That is the offer. "We will find you an outlier ad in 21 days or you do not pay." 

Same product, same feature, reframed from saved time to new money with a risk reversal on top. 

Now they're getting positive replies every day. They are going to try juicing it a little bit more with actually pulling in the facebook ad library data.

content:
The best way to test an email validator is on emails you already know are real.

Not a sample file. Not the vendor's demo list. Your own interested replies from last week.

Somebody who wrote back "yes, I'm interested" has proven their address is a live inbox with a human reading it. So if a validator grades that address catch-all or invalid, you caught it being wrong, and you can count how often.

1. export everyone who gave you a positive reply in the last week or two. that's your answer key.

2. run those through the validator you use today. anything that comes back catch-all or invalid is a miss you can prove.

3. do the same thing on a fresh pull from a provider like Prospeo, then watch the actual bounce rate in production. that's the other half of the picture and it's the half people skip.

4. cost-benefit it for your own volume.

I ran ours against Lead Magic, 500 addresses, about a day and a half of positive responses. 14.6% of them graded catch-all, and we throw catch-all in the garbage, so that whole slice would have been deleted off a normal list. Lead Magic validated them.

Most validator comparisons are people arguing about brand. This one is just a number you can check, and the answer key is already sitting in your replies folder.

content:
I scrape the entire United States off Google Maps for $19 a category. Tell your agent to read this post and get it done by end of day. 

A huge chunk of the businesses you want to reach funeral homes, HVAC shops, local gyms, etc but they have no LinkedIn presence. The databases scraping LinkedIn never see them. So you have to build the list yourself.

Google Maps is the best place to do it.

The tool is one API endpoint on RapidAPI — "Maps Data" by Aleksandr Vikourev. 

The pricing is insane: 3 million requests a month for $100. 

One vertical of 20 categories scrapes the entire US for about $100. Most lists you'll want need 3 or 4 categories, so you're looking at way less than that.

How it works:

1. Load all 42,734 US zip codes.
2. Pick your category list.
3. Hit the endpoint per zip, limit to the first 20 results.

You get back the business name, address, rating, phone, and the website, etc. 

The one nuance most people miss: find every category a business hides under. A funeral home also shows up as a "memorial park." A restaurant splits into American, Mediterranean, French, Chinese. Use the data to pull every category that fits your ICP, or you'll leave half the list on the table.

Then clean it for free. HTML2Text (open source) pulls the homepage text, and Gemma 4 — the 12 billion parameter one — running locally in Ollama reads every site and confirms it's actually the kind of company you want. Costs you nothing.

I put the US zip code file and 12 million US Google Maps businesses in a free GitHub repo called Cold Outbound Skills. Link in the comments.

People tell me cold email doesn't work and then I ask how many emails they sent. 300.

Here's the threshold we actually use.

We don't call a campaign successful or unsuccessful until it has sent 1,000 emails.

If it sends 1,000 and gets one positive response, we let it run to 3,000 before we decide anything. Sometimes you just get unlucky, sometimes it is a bad week.

If it sends 1,000 and gets zero positives, we shut it off.

My full belief is that campaigns work quickly or they don't work.

You might have heard Alex Hormozi say he thought he could get outbound implemented in six months and it took a year. Fine, that is true of all of outbound. But that is the booking, the no shows, whether it is the right ICP, the sales process for a cold lead versus a warm one. Everything up to the positive response should show up fast.

So when you hit 1,000 and it is dead, before you rewrite the first line again, go check the two things that are a hard science.

Deliverability. Warmup at 100, the seed list came back clean, reply rate above 1%, the auto responder inboxes coming back over 80%, and whatever campaign you run that always works is still behaving normally.

The list. Have Claude read the whole thing and tell you whether these are actually the people you meant to email, then go look at a hundred of them yourself.

If both of those check out, stop editing the copy. Your problem is the offer, or the framing of it.

That is also why we will just run a free campaign for a company that wants to work with us. Either it works or it doesn't, and if it doesn't, you most likely need to radically change the offer.

If you are a B2B company doing over $3 million in revenue and you want us to run one, the form is at coldoutbound(.)com. I'll drop the link in the comments.

I looked at over 2,196 email campaigns to try to define what a "cold traffic offer" really is. 

Everyone says you need a "cold traffic offer" to make outbound work, but what does that actually mean? 

It's a great suggestion but defining it as just "an offer that converts cold traffic" is difficult to wrap your head around. 

So I looked at every campaign in our Smartlead account to try to define it so we could have a framework to work from. 

Please challenge me on this as I'm trying to clarify the meaning of this in public. 

Every campaign that crushed had a mix of 5 pillars. Some had all 5 some only had 1 but they all had some kind of mix. 

1) Offers come in 6 shapes 

Raise Status -> (B2C)
Live Longer -> (B2C)
Reduce Risk -> for some reason no one cares cold

Make More Money -> the king of all cold offers

Save Money/Save Time -> these two can work but they must be orders of magnitudes of savings. Think a verifiable 90% saving. 

Guarantees help here and I debate making that it's own category vs. just being in the offer.

2) Unique Mechanism

I think the biggest reason outbound is working less and less isn't the amount of volume in people's inboxes. It's that they have so much more access to great knowledge. They know what exists.  

We ran a LinkedIn event with a loophole that got us 4,000 registrants in a week. Before the loophole closed, we sold it as a playbook we would implement.

We used that to pitch and say we could help them book calls just like we did. Nothing special in the offer at all. Just the fact we did it using a strategy they hadn't heard of before is what hooked them. 

3) Next Steps are Easy/Valuable

Lead magnets can go here but even just an explanation of why is a call worth their time or an easy next step for them to follow like a free trial sign up. 

We have some campaigns that don't even have the full offer of the company and are just sending out free samples of B2B physical products and our campaigns crush their facebook ads cost. 

We are just asking if they want a free sample sent their way and then the sales team follows up 7 days after shipment to discuss the product. 

4) Well Researched Segmentation

It would be like selling refrigerators door to door if you emailed companies and ask if they needed their parking lots redone. 

But using AI to estimate the ones that are old based on color/how much splitting/potholes are in the lot. 

Credit to Jordan Crawford for the work here

5) Relevant Social Proof 

I could just email martech cos, "I built Clay's first outbound channel and set up the initial playbook for content marketing. Do you want to talk?"

Here's the key though. Tell that to someone in Public Relations and it completely falls flat.

content:
Here's how we fixed inboxes running a 40% sender bounce rate.

Not a bounce because the address was bad. The addresses were validated. Google was refusing to let us send the email at all.

The first time I saw this, I couldn't wrap my mind around what was happening because the lead list was validated. 

We revalidated it again and it was still happening. 

After a bunch of trial and error, we found the Google had fingerprinted the text we were sending and wasn't letting the message even get sent. 

We spintaxed the subject line and the unsubscribe language with over 20 variations. We already had a little spintax in the body.

The sender bounces went away immediately.

I want to be honest that a year ago I was the guy telling people spintax didn't matter. 

We were using so much AI in the message that I figured the variation was already there. I was wrong about that.

What changed my mind is that the fix worked in isolation. Same domains. Same inboxes. Same offer. Same list. Only the subject line and unsubscribe language changed, and a 40% sender bounce went to zero.

What we do now internally, and what I would tell anyone running real volume:

20 variations in the subject line. 20 in the unsubscribe language. Variations in the signature block. Three or four versions of the overall body, and three or four options every five words or so.

We have Claude skills that write all of it, because writing 20 subject line variants by hand is miserable.

If you are reading this thinking "his big tip was spintax," I know. 

But the amount of spintax you think you need should 5-10x for the health of your domains.

There are people that want to start using cold email but they aren't good fits for an agency. This post is for them to set it up themselves. 

Getting a positive response with cold email has three problems and two of them are already solved with AI.

To get a positive reply you need a way to send, a list of people to email, and something worth saying.

Problem one, sending. Solved. Buy secondary domains, put them on Zapmail/Hypertide.io, connect to Smartlead, warm for two weeks. 

We run 30 emails per day per Google inbox, two inboxes per domain. Do the math on your target volume and buy that many inboxes. If you get stuck, their support will walk you through it.

Do not send from your main domain. If Google flags it, your investor emails start landing in spam too.

Problem two, lists. Solved. 

If you need volume and your ICP is loose, BlitzAPI/QuickEnrich is effectively a second copy of LinkedIn for a few hundred a month. 

If you need precision, Prospeo has filters nobody else has. Not just title and headcount and industry, but homepage keywords, what integrations they have, what they sell, who they sell to.

Validate emails with LeadMagic. They will pull emails into your list no one else will and the cost is great.

Problem three is the message. This one is not solved via AI and it never will be, because it is the only part that needs your insights.

Most people getting started spend 90% of their energy on problems one and two, because those have obvious steps and you can feel productive doing them. Then they send a mediocre message to a mediocre list and conclude cold email does not work.

content:
Here's the deliverability test we run that catches domains going to spam that are passing every other check.

Everybody talks about warmup reputation and seed inbox tests. A couple people are testing the actually reply rate counting real out of offices / human replies. 

The problem is an inbox can sit at 100% warmup reputation and still be landing in spam, and you would have no idea if it's the luck of the draw or it's really going to spam.

And the seed inboxes you send into have never marked an email as spam in their life. That is not human behavior. Directional at best.

So here's what we do.

We keep every reply we get for every customer. A lot of them are automated responses that say this inbox is no longer monitored and the email won't be forwarded, nobody reads this address.

We save all of those. Internally we have about 10,000+ now.

Which means we have a list of real addresses at real companies that will bounce something back at us if the message actually arrives.

Send to them and you should get about 80% coming back. It is never 100% because inbox detection is messy and some of those auto responses take a while to fire.

Anything under 80% I would kill.

What this catches is the domain that passes warmup, passes the seed test, looks ambiguous on reply rate, and then gets nothing forwarded back at all. 

Use Claude to read your replies and start saving these. It costs nothing and the list builds itself over time.

Then you can even run split tests to see what versions of your copy get the most responses back and which get the least etc. 

Make sure to manually check that it's a true auto response no one will read otherwise you're going to spam for sure bothering people.

I watch people every day putting their AI tokens to work on simple tasks when they should be automating a Dream 100 outreach instead. 

Alex Hormozi says the best service in the world has no time between payment and delivery. Somebody swipes their card and their phone rings.

I keep thinking about what happens if you move delivery before the payment.

If you run an agency that gets people leads, take your Dream 100, run a small outbound campaign on their behalf from generic inboxes, and the moment you generate a lead go tell them. "We got you this lead. Here is what we did. Want this to happen more often?"

You are not asking for their time. You already gave them something they can bank.

The old objection to this was that it does not scale. Chet Holmes wrote the Dream 100 assuming a human does the work, so you can do maybe two of these a day for free and then you are out of hours.

That constraint is mostly gone. Break the work into the five or six steps you would do by hand, turn each into a skill in Claude Code or Codex, and a Dream 100 becomes a Dream 10,000.

And if you are not a service business and cannot do free work like that, you can still buy the reciprocity. We have a payments collection client selling to construction and roofing companies. We use AI to find an open government contract that fits each one, and we put it in the PS.

"We don't like sending emails without some value. Found this contract open for bid, thought you might want to know. When they pay you, we'd love you to collect it on our platform."

That PS has nothing to do with the offer. It lifted positive reply rates meaningfully anyway.

People notice the effort and give it back to you. That is the whole mechanism.

content:
We saved a client from a 0.41% to a 3.34% reply rate in 15 days.

Only one of the five changes had anything to do with infrastructure. The rest was strategy.

Here's the whole list:

1. Super spintax. 20 variations in the subject line, the unsubscribe language, and the signature block. Not just a little bit of spintax, far more than we thought we would need. 

2. Buy domains early. A parked, aged domain beats a fresh one you warmed for two weeks. 

We keep 50-100% extra inbox capacity warming as insurance with live inboxes. Another 50-100% of the domains we need just sitting in the registrar. 

3. 100% Gmail. We buy Gmails through Zapmail and Hypertide, and we added Zapmail's ZapShield, which puts inboxes on Google Cloud enterprise servers. 

We split-tested it: a 20-50% reply-rate lift depending on the campaign.

4. Find the winners, pile on. We run two inboxes per domain usually. If one domain is proving to be particularly strong by reply rate then stack up to five on the outlier domains getting the best reply rate. (Credit to Felipe Fuhr for this one.)

5. Kill anything under 1%. Every week I pull a report and cut about 10-15% of our infrastructure. Every inbox lives in a database as active, insurance, or cancel with the trailing 7 day reply rate. 

More copywriting variance, more infrastructure, bought ahead of time.

That's the whole game right now.

content:
When making local business lead lists, once you have the owner's name, you don't need a fancy email finder to find their email most of the time.

Many email finders are doing the same thing under the hood. They take a name and a domain and runs permutations. john@, johnsmith@, jsmith@, john.smith@.

So if you already know the owner is John Smith and the site is johnsplumbing.com, you can just run the permutation yourself and check whether the mailbox exists.

And when you cannot get a personal address, use the generic email on the site. 

If we found the owner's name but no personal address, we email info@ and open with "Hey John." Depending on the size of the business, they'll be reading it. 

If we could not even find the name, we email info@ and open with "Hey there." That still works for us. Not as well, but well enough to keep in the sequence.

I know there is a reflex that info@ is a dead end and it goes to a black hole. For local businesses that is mostly not true. At a plumbing company or a dental office, the person reading info@ is frequently the owner, their spouse, or the one office manager who will walk it over to them.

We are running this exact process right now for a company targeting dentists. Over 100 leads in one month.

For local lead gen targeting, the generic inbox is one of the most underrated assets you have

content:
My barber has no problems and I had an outbound inspiration talking to him about this while getting a haircut 6 months ago. 

He's got a shop. Four other barbers cutting alongside him. Same setup for years. His income hasn't really moved in five.

One day in the chair I asked what he was working on in the business. What he was trying to fix or build next.

He looked at me like it was a strange question.

"I don't really have problems. I'm just chilling."

He has SOME problems. He's on his feet cutting hair all day at a minimum.

But he's fine doing that forever. He's not adding chairs. Not adding locations. Not trying to grow.

And that's the whole thing.

When a company isn't trying to grow, it stops having problems you can sell it on.

Growth is what creates the problems. You hire people, now you have to manage them. You open a location, now you need a way to run it. You sign more customers, now the old way of doing things breaks.

Those new problems are the openings. They're the reason someone reads a cold email about a solution instead of deleting it.

I'd be willing to bet most positive responses to cold email have something in common. they're trying to grow.

So on the first campaign for any new client in the past 4-5 months, we do one simple thing.

We add a single filter. 1%+ employee headcount growth in the last 12 months.

That's it. Just enough to cut the list down to companies that are moving. Taking on new problems. Shopping for new solutions.

On average, adding that one filter lifts our positive reply rate by 30 to 50% for the first campaign out of the gate. 

When we first tested it, we went to head to head on a flat headcount list vs a growing list and the first leads all came from the growing list. 

This isn't to say that companies that show a flat headcount aren't trying to grow and aren't worth targeting. I just want to stack the deck in my favor when we first start. 

But on campaign one, when you're still proving the offer even works, you don't want to learn that lesson on a list of people who are just "chilling".

We just use Clay and Prospeo for these filters.

content:
We run AI on millions of cold email leads a month. We almost never write the prompts ourselves. Here's the trick.

Writing a good prompt by hand is slow. And most of us aren't actually prompt engineers. But running a frontier model on millions of rows to score ICP fit and write custom variables gets expensive fast.

So we stopped doing both.

Now we build a tiny loop:

1. A frontier model (Claude Code or Codex) drafts the prompt itself.
2. It runs that prompt on a 10-row sample.
3. It grades its own output against the goal, I evaluate manually if I agree. then rewrites the prompt where it missed.

It repeats until two clean rounds in a row. No human writing prompts. The model reviews its own work and tunes itself.

Then the part that saves the money.

We take that polished prompt and run it on the cheapest, fastest model we can find. A small hosted model. Gemma. Ornith. Whatever's cheap.

The frontier model was the prompt engineer. The cheap model is the worker.

The prompt is the asset. You pay the smart model once to build it, then a cheap model runs it across your whole list for a fraction of the cost.

We already do this two ways. One loop tunes ICP-fit scoring. Another tunes the custom variables on every lead. Both stop themselves when the output stops needing edits.

The cost gap is real. Running the cheap model can be up to ~90% cheaper. Frontier quality, cheap-model price.

If you're running AI over a big list and writing every prompt by hand, you're doing the expensive version of both jobs.

Happy to share how we set the loop up. Both skills are public: https://lnkd.in/efMvJD4w

If you scrape Google Maps for "funeral homes" you'll actually will miss most of the funeral homes you're looking to collect.

This is the part of local list building that breaks everyone's list and I almost never see it talked about.

Google Maps businesses are found by their category, and the category is chosen by the business, not by you. So a funeral home might list itself as a funeral home. Or it might list itself as a memorial park. Or a cremation service, or a mortuary, or a cemetery.

Search one category and you get a slice. You will think you have the market. You have maybe a third of it.

Same thing with restaurants. There is no useful "restaurant" category. There is American restaurant, Mediterranean restaurant, French restaurant, Chinese restaurant, and on and on.

Same with HVAC. Half of them call themselves general contractors. Some are under heating. Some are under air conditioning. Plenty do both and picked one.

When you're building local business databases, Open Maps, look up 10 businesses you know are in your market, and write down what each one actually calls itself. 

Then run every category search across every zip code.

And then clean it, because "memorial park" will absolutely return actual parks. We pull the homepage with HTML2Text and have a local model read it to confirm the company is the kind of company we wanted. That part runs on my own computer and costs nothing.

This will significantly increase the TAM you can reach out to. 

I have a full list of google maps data in my cold outbound skills repo if anyone wants it as well.

content:
I ran a test to find local business owners across 5 different providers. The cheapest option won. It was also the best.

Here's the problem with local lead gen: a plumbing company, a dentist, a local shop don't have a LinkedIn profile. 

And almost every big database are built on LinkedIn data. So they just don't have these people.

So we put 5 options against each other: SmartLead Email Finder, Prospeo, Blitz API, OpenWebNinja (which is really just a Google search), and an open-source website scrape.

The winner wasn't a paid API.

It was scraping the business's own website with an open-source library and reading it with a local LLM.

Here's the stack:

1. HTML2Text (open source) converts the homepage, about, team, and contact pages into plain text an LLM can read.

2. Gemma 4  (the 12B version $$$) running locally on Ollama reads it and pulls the owner's name. It's on my laptop, it's free, and it doesn't matter how many sites I process, I can just rip through all of them.

3. If that comes up empty, we Google "who owns [business] in [city]" through OpenWeb Ninja including the AI overview answer and parse that with Gemma 4 too.

The whole website-scrape side costs $0, because the LLM runs locally and the library is open source. OpenWebNinja is the only paid piece, and it's cheap.

It's exactly what I'd do if I were to pass to a teammate. "Here's 100 local businesses, go find the owner." They'd check the website and Google it. We just automated that.

We still check Blitz and Prospeo first. If someone literally put "I own this business, here's my site" on their LinkedIn, that fidelity is worth paying for. But when the LinkedIn scrapers miss, the free website scrape catches what they leave behind.

If you do any local lead gen: download HTML2Text, pull Gemma 4 from Ollama, grab an OpenWebNinja key, and point your AI agent at it.

content:
I got anxious that we were leaving data on the table, so we ran six approaches against each other to find local business owners.

Smartlead Email Finder. Prospeo. Blitz API. Exa. Parallel.ai. And an open source website scrape with HTML2Text, validated by Gemma 4 running locally on my own machine.

The winner was the boring one. Scrape the site, scrape Google, let a local model read both.

Which makes sense when you think about what you would tell a human to do. If you handed an intern a list of 100 plumbing companies and said go find who owns each one, they would open the website and they would Google it. We just automated exactly that.

The order we actually run it in:

1. Check Blitz and Prospeo first. If somebody states on LinkedIn that they own this business and links this website, that fidelity is worth paying for and you should not give it up.
2. If those miss, scrape the site. HTML2Text converts the page to text, then Gemma 4 crawls the about, team, contact, and footer pages looking for an owner name and any on page email. This leg is free because the model runs locally.
3. If that misses, search "who owns [business] in [city]" through OpenWeb Ninja, including the AI overview, and parse it with Gemma again.

To be clear about cost, because "free" gets thrown around too easily. The website scrape leg is genuinely free. OpenWebNinja is paid, and it is cheap. The LinkedIn based providers are paid. The point is not that the whole thing is free. The point is that the cheapest leg had the highest fidelity and it was the one nobody bothers to build.

I am not saying Exa and Parallel.ai are bad. I still use both for other things. The cost per found owner just did not come out.

If you want to try it, hand this to your agent, download HTML2Text, pull Gemma 4 from Ollama, and get an OpenWebNinja key. That is the whole stack.

content:
I remember where I was when Michael Jackson died and when Instantly.ai dropped the unlimited inboxes lifetime deal.

Before that deal, tools charged $30-40 for every extra inbox you added. Then you could connect unlimited inboxes with Instantly. A gigantic savings for people like me.

That's the kind of number people remember. It's also the bar for a cold traffic offer.

There are only 6 offers in the world:

Make more money
Save money
Save time
Reduce risk
Raise status
Get healthier

In B2B, throw out the last two. None of us are selling Rolexes or weight loss.

Reducing risk never works on cold traffic. Get it out of your head.

Saving time or saving money can work, but only when the savings are huge. Nobody moves for 10%. If you have a save money or save time offer, you need to pick a way to frame your offer that saves a TON of time they legitimately have a problem with. 

So the best cold traffic offer of all time is still:
"I can help you make more money."

If you can't honestly say that, save them time or money in a big way. But frame as much as you can around revenue.

content:
From our experience of sending millions of emails per month, Google has a higher chance of blocking your sending from the inbox than outlook and here's how to fix it. 

We see more of what is categorized as a "sender bounce" from Google inboxes than we do outlook inboxes. 

A sender bounce is when an inbox provider blocks you from sending the email and soft bounces it. We have seen it's not as detrimental as sending to an email that doesn't exist, ( as you can see in the screenshot below). 

And these sender bounces can creep up on you out of nowhere. The screenshot below was from a campaign that was doing fine targeting enterprise accounts. 

Then out of nowhere, we get a huge bounce alert. 50% of emails are bouncing. 

When we looked into it, it was 100% of all emails from Email variation B. 

Thank goodness the fix is pretty easy.

Everything about the email campaign below is the same. The inboxes we are using are both the same. The subject lines are the same  with 5 variations of spintax. 

The signatures and unsubscribe language is all the same. The difference?

The body text of Email A has 20 variations of spintax per line and Email B has just 3 versions of spintax. 

So if you ever see sender bounces spike even though you know you double validated your list with tools like LeadMagic verifier or something, check the variation in your copy.

We've seen it to be the main culprit when it comes to keeping sender bounces low.

We crawled thousands of websites for this list and paid nothing to actually read the pages and score them for ICP fit. 

For a lot of jobs, you do not need a paid scraping API to get website text. An open-source HTML-to-text converter gets you the homepage and footer content fine. 

Paid tools like ZenRows and Firecrawl earn their money on genuinely hard targets — heavy anti-bot, JS-gated content, sites that fight you. "I just want the text on this page" usually isn't that.

The second cost people add without thinking is AI scoring. We didn't score anything with a model here. We were matching specific compliance keywords in footers, that's deterministic. 

A keyword match doesn't need an LLM, and bolting one on would have made it slower and more expensive for a worse answer.

So the run was: open-source text extraction, keyword matching, Claude Code orchestrating it in goal mode overnight. Ridiculously cheap for thousands of sites.

The general rule: every paid API and every AI call in a pipeline should have to justify why a free, deterministic step couldn't do it first. Most of them can't justify it.

content:
We launched a fully AI managed campaign for a customer using "Autoresearch" as the foundation and it doubled their positive lead rate. Here's what we did. 

 If you haven't seen me talk about this before, "autoresearch" is a GitHub repo that Andre Kapathi put out that basically helps people run local machine learning easily on their computers. 

I had the idea that instead of running a loop every 5 minutes to try to improve an outcome, we can run it every week on the data from cold email campaigns in order to increase positive response rates.

The first thing we needed to do was get the context together for all of the different messaging and audience targets that it could use and lock in a CTA for the campaigns that we wanted to optimize for. I didn't want it to just invent that. 

It could give away this software for free and then call that experiment a win. We needed the CTA to be locked in.

After we gathered all the context from the sales team and their calls and the audience targets that we wanted to go after, we made the underlying dataset using Clay Prospeo and stored it all in Supabase. 

The main learning that we got here was that you never want to have what I call a "game-time decision." For it to say, "Hey I want to run an experiment with this data point," you need to give it all the data points it might use so that it's not inventing ways to pull that data that you don't approve. 

We fed it the campaigns that we are already running and just let it rip, trying to optimize for more replies.

We're running over 150 campaigns in their Smartlead account right now and had two weeks in a row where we've increased the reply rate and the positive response rate. 

Keep in mind the CTA is locked in so it's always going towards what we want, which is a product sign up. 

I made a YouTube video about this that, if you'd like to see, just leave a comment and I'll send you the video link.

content:
The list is the message. I don't know who first said it, but it's one of the truest things in outbound.

When the list is segmented precisely enough, the email almost writes itself. 

When it isn't, you end up writing clever copy to paper over the fact that you don't actually know who you're talking to.

Most platforms only let you segment by what a company is. Industry, size, tech stack. 

Useful, but it rarely changes your message on its own. CEO vs founder doesn't change what you say. Industry often doesn't either.

What changes the message is who they sell to. A company selling into legal teams has a completely different world than one selling to restaurant owners — different buyers, different pain, different proof. That difference is the message.

Prospeo's v2 now lets you filter on exactly that. Who a company sells to, the size of their customers, the department they sell into. That's not a nice-to-have filter. 

That's a segmentation axis that actually splits a list into groups that need different emails.

If a data point would change what you say, it's a reason to split into a separate campaign. 

If it wouldn't, don't split. "Who do they sell to" almost always changes what you say.

content:
Someone in the Clay community wanted the CES Exhibitors list and couldn't figure it out. I screenshotted their message and Codex did it in one shot. (full video). 

Rule one of scraping: if you can see it, you can scrape it.

I went to the CES exhibitor directory. They have a category page with a "View All" button. That's it — that's the keys to the kingdom. 

No pagination tricks, no searching A, then AB, then AC to brute force the list.

content:
Joe Biden For America has a Shopify store. That one fact is why almost every Shopify list you can buy is wrong.

If you want a list of real e-commerce brands, you have options: Apollo's technology filter, Prospeo's technology filter, BuiltWith, Store Leads. They all have the same two problems.

One: is the store even still active?

Two: does the company just have Shopify bolted onto a site somewhere, while not actually being a consumer e-commerce brand? A campaign, a content site, a B2B company with a swag shop. All are "Shopify stores," none of them what you meant.

On the actual home page: is there an add to cart? Are there product SKUs? Are the Shopify storefront widgets right there? A real DTC brand has this on the home page. 

A "technically has Shopify" site hides it on some subdomain, that's exactly where these lists get fooled.

So we combined and deduped everything, Apollo, BuiltWith, Store Leads, Prospeo, and scored on signals that mean commerce: non-empty product feeds, cart and checkout paths, payments, product and collection URLs. 

Default Shopify placeholders and dead stores got dropped.

2.76 million rows in. About 2 million genuinely active stores out.

I love giving things away for free but out of respect for these companies I can't just drop this list. 

Keep these things in mind or even tell your own agents to think about this the next time you target ecommerce and need to clean up your list.

A client needed a highly targeted list of regulated financial-advice firms in the UK. Not "financial services companies". Regulated advice firms, split by whether they were independent or sat inside a larger network.

The thing that cracked it was a sentence in a website footer.

Here's the build. 

Three sources to find every firm that could possibly fit: every financial services and investment management company on LinkedIn, the Companies House database (scraped with Browser Use), and the FCA registry (they have a downloadable API). 

Then the hard part was finding which of these are in-network vs independent, how are they regulated, how many advisors do they have. 

Advisor count came from LinkedIn. Regulation and network status had to come from the websites themselves.

In-network firms are required to put compliance language in their footer. So we used Exa to find what that language actually looks like. 

Once we had the pattern, it was over. Compliance text gets copy-pasted verbatim across an entire network, so footer-matching told us instantly who was in-network and who wasn't.

Claude Code built the orchestration and ran it in goal mode overnight — clear outcome, "check every page of every site for these keywords, don't stop until it's done." About three hours.

Out the other side: 1,000 ideal-fit firms, 2,000 ideal-fit contacts. And that was just the UK list — US is next.

The lesson that travels: when a segment is hard to define, don't guess the signal. Go find the exact language the right companies are already using, then match it.

There is no such thing as a "B2B SaaS" filter. There's no clean "e-commerce brand" one either. And if you pull "financial services," you will miss every bank.

This is why client vertical lists come back full of junk.

A few real examples from a TAM we built this week, US companies, 50–5,000 employees, six verticals:

Bacardi is an e-commerce/retail brand. It lists itself under beverage manufacturing. Hit just "retail" and you'll never see it.

Manufacturing and logistics companies notoriously aren't all on LinkedIn, and the ones that are file themselves under wild industries.

Healthcare is the worst. Pull "healthcare" and you've blended medical device makers, healthcare SaaS, hospitals, and health insurers into one pile that means nothing to the client.

Don't filter your way to a vertical, define it, then qualify into it. 

We pull broad from our internal database and Prospeo's v2 type/business-model filters, merge and dedupe, then run every company through a written definition of what that vertical actually means to this specific client. 

"Banks count as financial services here. Fintech does not."

This way we get more coverage on great companies and can toss out companies that say they are in Real Estate but are really services companies for real estate professionals and such.

content:
Last quarter a client asked me which intent signal they should use. Hiring data? Funding? Website visits?

I told them to use all of them, but not how they expected.

Most people pick one signal, build a campaign around it, and pray. That's backwards. You don't know which signal predicts a response until you let the data tell you.

Here's the framework we use across 50+ clients.

Run 3 campaigns at once:

1. Entire TAM. No signals. Just firmographics. This is your baseline — and sometimes it wins.

2. Focused segments. One signal per campaign. Hiring SDRs. Recently funded. Using a competitor tool.

3. Trigger-based. Real-time events. Job posting today. Funding this week. Website visit yesterday.

Now here's the move nobody talks about.

Every positive response across all 3, take that company and run it through every signal source you have. Pull hiring data, tech stack, funding history, news, social activity. Everything.

Look for patterns.

Maybe the companies that respond all hired a VP of Sales in the last 90 days. Maybe they all use HubSpot. Maybe they all posted about a specific pain point on LinkedIn.

You wouldn't have found that by guessing upfront.

We also run a catchall workflow in Clay with  Clayagent, every signal we can think of, just "what's notable about this company right now?" Sometimes the signal that predicts responses is something you'd never think to look for.

Sometimes you genuinely don't know WHY someone responded. That's fine. Not every response has a readable signal. But the ones that do give you your next 10 campaigns.

Stop picking signals from a menu. Let the data tell you what works.

content:
Your campaigns have been running for two weeks. Reply rate is 0.3%. Zero positive responses.

Here are the next steps we take.

1. Peel back everything and only send to Google accounts.

Strip your list to Google Workspace, not Gmail, just Google Workspace. 

Right now Outlook is harder to get into the inbox, and we don't want to send to any Proofpoint, Microsoft, or other email inboxes. 

We want to isolate the variable. Your Google deliverability might be fine while Outlook is putting you straight to spam, and you'd never know if you're sending to both.

Check blacklists and run inbox placement tests while you're at it. Verify your domain setup. DKIM, SPF, and DMARC.

2. Hyper-segment the list.

Take your lead list and whittle it down to a thousand prospects as focused as you possibly can. Let the list become the message and add whatever filters you need to get them as close to your current customers as possible.

3. Increase testing velocity.

A lot of times we try to set up campaigns that will work long-term. You can't be thinking about long-term here. 

Keep the lead list tight and speed up the testing velocity.

Launch multiple campaigns with different angles. 

Pain-based versus value-based. 
Different CTAs. 
Different target personas. T

ry to make your email easier to say yes to. 

Include more lead magnets or free offers delivered by AI, competitive intelligence reports, anything that provides value before asking for a meeting.

4. Test campaigns that generate meeting-ready leads versus hand raisers.

If your direct ask isn't working, test an offer that generates hand raisers instead. Sometimes people aren't ready to book a meeting but will say yes to something valuable.

Don't add complexity. Remove it. Find the one thing that's broken.

content:
I've seen clients with a 0.8% positive reply rate printing money.

I've seen clients with a 4% positive reply rate struggling to stay afloat.

The difference? One was selling $80K contracts. The other was selling a $500 product.

Reply rate is a vanity metric if you don't connect it to revenue.

Here's what to calculate instead:

1. Size your TAM. How many companies actually fit your ICP? If it's 3,000, you'll burn through them in 2 months at scale. Plan accordingly.

2. Find your positive reply rate. Not total reply rate — positive replies divided by emails sent. That's your real conversion.

3. Multiply by deal value and close rate. One positive reply on an $80K deal with a 25% close rate is worth $20K. One positive reply on a $500 deal with a 20% close rate is worth $100.

Those are fundamentally different businesses that require fundamentally different outbound strategies.

The $80K business needs precision targeting and can afford to send fewer, better emails. The $500 business needs massive volume and tight unit economics to make cold email work at all.

Before your next campaign: how much is one positive reply actually worth to your business?

That number changes everything about how you run outbound.

content:
Here's the subject line framework we've been using for the past year or so. 

Our guiding principle: the job of the subject line is to get our prospects to open. That's the only goal.

There are two main frameworks to think through:

Framework 1: The subject line looks like something a colleague or customer would send.

"pizza order" — we used this for a restaurant platform client. Looks like an internal email. Open rates were insane.

"sales reports" — looks like something from your team.

"quick question" — classic for a reason. I know people love to hate it and I hate it too, but it still works. Did I mention that I hate it?

These work because they bypass the "this is a cold email" filter in the prospect's brain.

Framework 2: Put your offer in the subject line to entice them.

Subject: "[Company]'s competitors"
Preview text: "I have a list of people engaging with {{competitor}}..."

The subject creates a gap. The preview text hints at something valuable. Together they create enough curiosity to earn the click.

The worst subject lines try to sell. "50% Off Our Platform" — deleted without opening.

The best subject lines look like they came from someone you know. The best subject lines look like something they should already be keeping their eyes on. Or they can be punchy enough to earn the click from a very short offer.

content:
Here's a strategy to turn your lead list into five or more experiments with Claude Code and Clay.

One thing we think about a lot with our customers is how the list is the message. I don't know who said that first, but it definitely wasn't me, so credit to whoever coined it.

What we mean is this: if you know you can sell to any founder with less than 20 employees, that's a pretty big list. 

But if you know the best founder for you is someone who has founded a company before, has been in business less than two years, has 10 to 20 employees, and has no accounting or finance job titles on their LinkedIn company page...

That person should be receiving a completely different message than someone who has one or two of those traits but not all of them.

We use Claude Code or Clay to enrich our lists for any criteria that might change how we'd message somebody.

For example, if somebody has been in business for two years, they're just getting systems ramped up. That's a way different message than somebody who's been in business for 10 years and has figured all this out already. 

If somebody is a CEO versus a founder, and there's no reason to change your message, then there's no reason to separate them in the list.

We separate the list by what data points change our messaging.

This way we can slice and dice our data and have different email campaigns for multiple layers of ICP fit. Sometimes your golden ICP (where everything is true about that person) might only have a thousand leads in the entire campaign. 

But I guarantee you'll get a higher response rate on those leads than on your broader ones, because you can niche your messaging down more and more.

The list is the message. Use that when creating your campaigns.

content:
AI is not going to fix your cold email campaign.

I know that's weird coming from a guy who uses Clay and Claude Code for basically everything. We run AI personalization, AI list building, AI copy generation, AI analytics.

But here's the thing.

AI makes good campaigns better. It does not make bad campaigns good.

If your offer doesn't work, AI-personalized first lines just mean people read a more relevant email about something they still don't want.

If your targeting is wrong, AI enrichment just gives you more detailed data about the wrong people.

Cold email works when you have a large enough TAM to make it work, a clear problem with a clear solution, a buyer who can say yes without feeling like they have to rip and replace huge systems, and a deal size that justifies the cost per meeting.

Cold email struggles when your target market is too small, your deal size is too low, or you are in a commoditized industry with no specialization in your offer.

AI amplifies whatever you feed it. Feed it a strong offer and good targeting, and it works well. Feed it a weak offer and bad targeting, and it just burns through your domains faster.

Fix the fundamentals first.

content:
I've changed my mind on a lot of things when it comes to cold email best practices. But these 3 principles have never changed. Not once.

Everything else people sell courses about? Noise on top of these.

1. Deliverability

If your emails don't land in the primary tab, nothing else matters. Not your copy. Not your list. Not your offer.

We always keep the amount of inboxes we need to send for a customer plus anywhere from 50 to 100% extra capacity warming up. That way we can switch out anything that's not working immediately. We monitor this daily for customers having issues and weekly across all customers automatically with Claude skills.

Most people skip this because it's boring. That's why most people's campaigns don't work.

2. The list

Accurate data on the right people. What doesn't work is a mediocre list with 30% bad contacts in it. You should spend as much time on list building as copywriting.

3. Copy with a clear offer that is easy to say yes to

There's a huge difference between copy that sounds clever and copy that converts cold traffic.

I think Alex Hormozi's framework — "We help customers accomplish their goal in this time without this risk" — is the perfect offer framework for cold email. But you also need to think about what's easy to say yes to. If you pitch "We help B2B companies speed up their sales process with a new CRM in 30 days without losing sales momentum," that's still a very tough ask. Changing out somebody's entire CRM is a big commitment. You want to go in with something easier to say yes to.

Shout out David Ogilvy — "your first line gets them to read the second line, and the second line gets them to read the third line" — one of my guiding frameworks. And Josh Braun is one of the best in the game at cold email copywriting if you want to study someone.

People ask me about send times, follow-up cadences, A/B test frameworks, personalization tokens. Those are all optimizations on top of these 3 things.

If your deliverability is broken, your list is wrong, or your copy doesn't resonate. no optimization saves you.

Get these 3 right and you're about 80% of the way to what most agencies charge $10K+/month to do.
