content:
Your lead lists have more garbage in them than you think. And here's how you can work on fixing it.

The problem comes down to three things:

1. The data is scraped from self-reported data that people mislabel.

Companies are notoriously bad at putting the correct industries on LinkedIn. Someone marks themselves as "Information Technology" when they're really a logistics company with a website. You need to look at their actual websites and company descriptions and use AI to verify fit — not just trust the label.

2. The data is possibly outdated.

You need to figure out when the data was last updated from your provider. If it's stale, you need to either scrape Google for current information or get a more expensive data provider that will pull the data live. That "150-person startup" might have gone through layoffs and now has 12 people. Or got acquired.

3. Data providers can't predict every use case.

What counts as a "B2B SaaS company" versus an "e-commerce company"? Some people say e-commerce is any company with a Shopify store. But Biden for America was built on Shopify. Your definition of ICP doesn't match the category labels that data providers use.

You have to build a layer on top of their data to work with this.

Here's how we fix it:

For the self-reported data problem, use AI to look at websites and company descriptions to make a real fit determination. Show AI what 30 good companies look like, then keep editing your prompt until it gets all 30 correct. Then run it on everything.

For outdated data, check when it was last updated. If it falls outside your range, scrape or pay for live data.

For the use case problem - use Claude Code or Codex with the batch API to throw as much AI inference at it as possible. Rent GPUs if you have to. This is a problem that AI has made solvable for the first time.

The data will never be perfect. But you can get a lot closer than most people think.

content:
Most people use LinkedIn outbound wrong.

Where people are getting it wrong is they think: email somebody, then connect with them on LinkedIn the next day, then follow-up email, then LinkedIn message. 

That sounds great in theory. But the math just doesn't work out. 

The volume you can send on email versus connection requests you can send on LinkedIn is completely different.

Instead, we want to create an order of operations where we're reaching out to the most engaged, highest likelihood to reply leads first.

1. Engaged leads from your other channels. Automate connecting and reaching out to any person who is an engaged lead, inbound forms, cold email replies, ad responders, whatever. 

These people already showed interest somewhere. LinkedIn is your follow-up.

2. De-anonymized website visitors. Anybody visiting your website who was identified with your favorite de-anonymization platform like Snitcher or Visual Visitor. 

They were looking at you. Now go find them.

3. People in your ICP engaging with your current customers. As long as you have marketing rights, reach out and mention that you work with that company. 

When you name-drop the case study, they know exactly who you're talking about.

4. Your competitors' LinkedIn engagement. Connect with and message people commenting on and reacting to your competitors' posts. These people care about the category. They're already educated.

5. Your golden ICP. After all of the above, then go cold to your best-fit prospects.

By the time you go through these five tiers, it's going to be another month gone by, and you have more engagers to reach out to, more website visitors, more competitor activity to scrape. The cycle repeats.

This is a much better strategy than blasting your connection requests at a cold list.

content:
If your campaign is getting decent out of office / negative reply rates, people are clearly reading, and nobody's responding positively, there's a good chance you're raising an objection you're not addressing. 

And you'll never know it because the prospect won't tell you.

They just delete. 

Every cold email creates an implicit pushback in the reader's mind.

"We help companies scale outbound" — they think "I already have an agency."

"We reduce your cloud costs by 40%" — they think "Switching sounds like a nightmare."

They read. They think the objection. They're gone.

Read your own email like a skeptical buyer. What's the first pushback? Now address it in one sentence. Not defensively. Casually.

"We help companies scale outbound (most of our clients already had an agency, we work alongside them, not replace them)"

"We reduce cloud costs by 40% (no migration required, we optimize your existing setup)"

One sentence. Inserted naturally. Kills the objection before it fully forms.

But don't start here.

If your targeting is wrong, objection preemption won't save you. If your offer is weak, addressing objections just highlights the weakness. And critically — don't bring up objections the prospect wasn't thinking about. If you're selling accounting services and you write "even though we're a small firm," you just planted doubt that didn't exist.

This is an advanced move. Use it when you've validated the campaign is reaching the right people, they're reading, and something in the copy is creating friction.

content:
I don't write prompts for list qualification anymore. Instead, I use a skill I call it the ICP prompt loop.

I tell Codex (or Claude Code): "This is the input I'll give you. This is the output I want. Write the prompt that makes that happen." 

Then I feed it what we actually mean by giving it human verified data. 

"This is what we count as a B2B SaaS company, this is what we count as manufacturing, this is what financial services means to this client, and so on"

Then it runs on 10 real companies and shows me its work: "This one is B2B SaaS. This one we thought was, but isn't, and here's why. This one is manufacturing and I agree."

I correct it. It revises the prompt.

The rule that makes it work: it does not get to run across the full dataset until it shows me 10 companies with zero edits from me, three times in a row. 

One edit anywhere and the counter resets. It keeps feeding me 10 at a time until we get three clean rounds.

This week we used it on a 6-vertical TAM. Sonnet 4.6 on the batch API did the actual qualification for about $50 because there were too many companies for task sub-agents.

This way, you stop guessing whether your prompt is good and start proving it on the only thing that matters, real rows from your actual list.

content:
Here's something nobody talks about in cold email deliverability.

Your offer quality directly affects whether you land in the inbox.

Not indirectly. Directly.

Here's the cycle:

Bad offer → nobody replies → email providers see zero engagement → they assume you're spam → more emails go to junk → even fewer replies → inboxes burn faster → you buy more domains → those burn too.

Now flip it:

Good offer → people reply → email providers see real engagement → you stay in the inbox → more people see your emails → more replies → inboxes last longer → you need fewer domains → your costs drop.

This is why two agencies can run the exact same infrastructure 

Same warmup tool, same sending volume, same ESP, same domain setup 

But get completely different deliverability results.

One has offers people respond to. One doesn't.

We manage deliverability across 50+ clients at GrowthEngineX. Same Smartlead setup, same inboxes, same warmup schedules. The clients with the best deliverability are not the ones with the fanciest technical setup.

They're the ones with the best offers.

Every time someone asks me "how do I fix my deliverability" my first question is "what's your reply rate?"

If it's under 1%, your deliverability problem might be an offer problem.

Fix the offer and watch the technical metrics fix themselves.

It's a virtuous cycle when it's working. And a death spiral when it's not.

content:
If you're thinking about using cold email because you think it's another touch that will increase the ROI on other channels, you're looking at it the wrong way.

I've seen this play out dozens of times.

Early on in my career, companies would work with us and say, "Hey, even if we don't get replies, at least we're getting our name in front of them."

I used to say, "OK sure, we can do that." Send them the invoice. They'd pay and then cancel the next month because they weren't seeing any real attribution.

Here's the thing: cold email doesn't damage your brand (probably a whole post can be made about this) but it also doesn't build your brand.

I always ask people this: what was the most recent cold email that you received an hour ago?

Nobody can remember. At all.

Cold email doesn't have as many risks as people might believe to damage your brand as long as you follow the rules and follow best practices. 

Don't ignore unsubscribe requests. Don't follow up 12 times. Don't email people about products they literally built.

But on the flip side, I'm also very confident that it doesn't positively increase your brand either.

It's one of the only marketing styles that is really direct response and doesn't leave lasting impressions on people. For better or worse.

That's just my experience with it after 5 years and 8 million emails a month.

If you want brand awareness, invest in content and community. If you want pipeline, use cold email. They're different tools for different jobs.

content:
The most common thing I hear from founders: "Cold email doesn't work for my business."

5 years of doing this, I've never found a business where some version of cold email doesn't work. The problem is what you're trying to accomplish with cold email, not the channel.

When people say "cold email doesn't work for my business," what I hear is: "cold email isn't helping me grow revenue." I think they're picking the wrong kind of outbound.

There are 3 types:

Type 1: Meeting-ready leads

Direct ask. "Want to save 40 hours/month on bookkeeping?" → "Yes, let's talk."

Works when the prospect already knows they have the problem. Accountants, agencies, SaaS with obvious pain points. You just need to show up at the right time.

Type 2: Hand raisers

Give value first. "I built a list of 200 companies engaging with your competitors on LinkedIn. Want it?"

Works when the prospect doesn't know they have a problem yet. Complex sales, high-trust products. You're not asking for a meeting. You're starting a conversation by providing something useful upfront.

Type 3: Partners, recruiting, and affiliates

Not selling. Connecting. "We send 8 million emails a month and need deliverability partners" or "We're hiring SDRs who want to learn at scale."

This is the most underused cold email funnel. Nobody thinks of recruiting or partnerships as cold email use cases, but the mechanics are identical.

I think every business should be using cold email. It just matters: can it work to get you meeting-ready leads? Can it work to get you hand raisers? Or does it work to help you build partnerships, affiliates, and recruit new employees?

And how much energy can you spend converting a meeting-ready lead to a deal closed versus a hand raiser to a deal closed versus a partner or affiliate?

I used to worry about silly things in my cold email campaigns. 5 years later, this is what I worry about and what I don't worry about. 

1. Which tool I'm sending from. My brother and sisters in outbound, the underlying technology of how Smarltead and Instantly send email is the largely the same. Pick who you like the feature set of more and move on. 

2. Does email warmup work and what are the perfect warmup settings. 

If email warmup didn't work, the platforms offering it unlimited for free would be the first people to ask you to shut it off so they could lower their AWS bill. 

I don't think there are perfect email warmup settings. As long as it's sending something and getting replies back it's fine. 

3. Triple Validating Leads

We validate our emails with million verifier before sending and enjoy the usage of bounce ban verified emails by using the Prospeo API. It's all going to be alright. 

4. Spam words in my copy. 

Ok if you send "Bitcoin" or "jesus" or "oprah" you're going to have issues. But I see people asking questions in chats all the time about the word free or something. And it's ok in moderation. If you think you're having issues, pull it out and see if it improves. 

5. The quest for email deliverability knowledge that no one else has. 

Any gimmick or strategy outside of the tried an true things we talk about on here all the time turns out to be a quick fad if it works at all or really not true. 

6. 3rd party tools to tell if you're emails are going to spam

Just check the reply rates of your domains...

7. Focusing on everything all at once in the copywriting vs spending 80% of my time on how I pitched the offer of what I'm helping to promote

8. Wondering if different email providers get better results than the others. Of course we use Hypertide.io and Zapmail.ai but if the provider you're using is fast and gives you access to the admin console, you're all set. 

9. This might not fit as a worry, but you should run more tests than you think and see how the best brands run facebook ads. It's no different. Cold email is just a private ads network. 

10. Working with a client where their website/case studies/social content wasn't dialed in.

content:
Before you write a single email, there's one question that determines everything — your copy, your CTA, your follow-up sequence, your entire funnel.

Most people skip it and wonder why their campaigns underperform.

The question: Can I ask for the meeting directly, or do I need to earn the right to ask?

That's the difference between generating meeting-ready leads and generating hand raisers.

A meeting-ready lead is someone who responds to your cold email and says "yes, let's talk next week." They're ready to book.

A hand raiser is someone who says "yes" to a lead magnet or a Loom video. They're interested, but they are not ready to meet with you right now. They require much more follow-up and warming before you book the meeting.

I see too many people going wrong here. They start using lead magnets, get excited about the response rates, and then try to immediately book meetings,  forgetting that not everyone is ready after one touchpoint. 

Everyone should try to start with getting meeting-ready leads. But if you can't, maybe your offer is very cyclical and prospects are locked into contracts, or it's a commoditized offering and you need to differentiate, you're going to run into problems. That's when you pivot to hand raisers.

Here's what we do at GEX. We offer a free campaign launch before people become customers. That generates meeting-ready leads. But when we paired that with a follow-up email offering to share a list of every new hire on LinkedIn or all the people engaging with their competitors' content — notified monthly — we 5x'd our response rates.

Sometimes it's not even one or the other. Email one goes for the meeting-ready lead. Email two follows up with a hand-raiser offer. Layer them together.

Which approach are you running right now?

content:
There is actually a limit to cold email reply rates.

Knowing this can hopefully free you from testing things that won't matter.

Let me explain.

I have worked with customers in the past that are obsessed with getting the reply rate as high as possible. They think if they send a good enough email, every single person who could possibly see it is going to respond.

We've run tests that show this just isn't the case.

We had the opportunity to work on behalf of Forbes at Web Summit. We had the list of speakers. We had all their emails. We cold emailed them from infrastructure that had warmed up for four months. The pitch was simple: "This is our booth. We want to interview you for Forbes. Book a meeting." And we sent them a link to Forbes.com.

That only got a 30% reply rate. Basically all positive.

When I say "only" 30% — if I were a speaker at an event and Forbes wanted to interview me, I would think the reply rate would be even higher than that.

We also helped a customer email their own customers. We found data that showed they needed a new product, and we could fix the problem for free.

Still only a 10% reply rate.

I say all this because these two examples are pretty undeniably good offers. And they still did not get 40, 50, 60% reply rates.

When you're sending emails, there are so many reasons why somebody doesn't respond. They didn't even see it. It got mixed up with everything else in their inbox. It's just not the right time for them.

When you've run a couple of experiments and the reply rate is staying pretty steady, I would think more about experiments around lists and experiments around offers versus trying to change the copy to see if an AI personalization or a fancier way of saying something is going to move the needle.

List segmentation and changing your offer matter way more.

What experiments have you run that changed your thinking on reply rates?

A 3 tier tech stack to build lists of your TAM from beginner to advanced to build niche lists and lists over 100,000 contacts. 

To build a 100,000+ contact database without manually searching anything, you need three things:

1) A daily driver that's your go to
2) A deep TAM builder
3) An always-running background scraper to custom find your particular data. 

Here’s how I’d approach each one 👇

Tier 1: Prospeo.io (Daily Driver)

Customer asks for a list?

First thing we do is hit the Prospeo API.

Results are nearly identical to LinkedIn

The API is stupid easy to work with

This handles ~80% of requests without touching anything else.

Fast. Cheap. Reliable.

Tier 2: Internal Company Database (or just use Clay) + Contact Waterfall

This is for when you need the full TAM and you need deeper company filters. 

We maintain a Supabase database with every company in the US enriched through Clay.

Clay gives us AI-derived fields most people don’t even realize exist:

Do they make subscription revenue?
Are they B2B?
What sub-industry are they in?
Local company or national?

Once we have the expanded list of companies, we run them through Prospeo, Clay People Source, Blitz API and Smartlead's new contact finder to get all contacts. 

Tier 3: Sales Navigator/Google Maps Scraper (Autopilot)

This is the long-term edge.
We run a Sales Navigator scraper via RapidAPI with cron jobs firing every single morning.

75,000 companies/day
75,000 contacts/day

Dedupes on website or LinkedIn URL

Focused on:
Newly founded companies (2024–2026)
Newly created roles
Accounts posting in the last 90 days

Most people use these tools when they have a project.

We run them constantly in the background.

New companies.
New people.
Every single day.

By the time a customer asks for more contacts, we already have them.

At this point, you’re about 80% of the way to a TAM that many agencies would happily charge $10k+ to build. And you did it without manual searching.

I think most people are wasting their LinkedIn outreach thinking of it like email instead of it's own channel. Here's the 3 strategies I'd do instead. 

I was speaking to James Winter about some suggestions I had for his portcos with Claude code and such and I brought up how one of their portcos wanted to sync LinkedIn outreach with email. 

"We think if we email them twice, we should move over to LinkedIn."

In my opinion, that's a waste of the channel. 

LinkedIn outreach (especially using voice notes) 99/100 times has higher reply rates than cold email but lacks the ability to scale without fake accounts. 

If you only had 25-50 connection requests to send per day, why would you use the same strategy of email where the channel scales linearly. 

When you're doing LinkedIn outreach, I'd focus on these things first. 

1) Use a tool like Trigify.io or some Rapid API endpoints to find your ICP engaging and connecting with customers you have permission to name drop. 

Find everyone engaging with your customer's employees posts and their company page.

Don't say, "I saw you engaging with my customer's post" but instead send your regular message you usually would but leave a custom variable in your social proof line of your message to reference that customer.

Instead of sending a message saying, "We help companies like {{company they have never heard of}}...." you can name drop that customer case study who they will of course know. 

2) Install every website deanonymization software on your site with a free trial. if they do contact lookup, clean them up and make sure they are ICP. If they do company lookup, use Clay or Prospeo.io to find contacts. 

Target people and companies with a high likelihood of being on your site. 

Again, don't mention anything about being on the site. Just reach out like you normally would and put a little delay on it. 

Track which tools give you the highest reply rates/success and pay for them. 

Probably a whole post can be dedicated on why I suggest you try them all for your niche but it's free, so trust me on this one. 

3) Reach out to people showing intent about your solution/problem/they are doing research/etc by targeting people in your ICP engaging with posts on the topic (or your competitor's post....) 

Same strategy here, just going a little bit more broad and using the last amount of capacity you'll have because of the limits of reaching out from 1 account. 

So instead of thinking about LinkedIn as an extension of email, remember you only get so many shots on goal and the reply rates are so much higher on LinkedIn. Use them to reach out to some of your hottest leads.

Cache the input for 90% off. Batch API for 50% off the call.

content:
If there are first-time founders out there that need to start cold email for zero dollars, this is how I would do it.

There are four problems you need to solve: deliverability, list building, copywriting, and sending. Let's take each as a checklist.

**1. Deliverability.**
It's not best practice, and I wouldn't even say it comes across as professional, but if you want to do cold email for zero dollars, sending from your personal email address will do the trick until you close enough deals to invest. Your personal email likely has years of reputation on it, and it will work fine for the low-volume use case we're going to do here.

**2. List building.**
You need a way to build lists and store them. You could save files locally and use the free tiers of Codex or Claude Code to do research and find 50 contacts to reach out to. If you need their emails, most email platforms have great free trials you could work between. Start a Prospeo free trial, for instance.

3. Copywriting.
Any ChatGPT or Claude instance can help you get started for free. I would suggest creating cold emails in the style of Josh Braun if you really don't know what to do here. His frameworks are simple and they work.

4. Sending.
A new repo was just dropped that controls your browser, and you could use the "send later" function inside of Gmail to do the sending. It cuts a couple corners here and there, but if you have absolutely no money to get started, this is how you'd be able to do it.

Now here's the progression when you're ready to invest:

$50/month: Smartlead or Instantly for sending + scheduling. They have built-in lead databases.

$200/month: Add 3-5 domains and inboxes. Buy a list from Prospeo or Clay. Use Million Verifier to clean it.

$500/month: I'd just invest in more domains and inboxes at this level. A/B testing across segments.

$2,000+/month: Waterfall enrichment. Intent signals. 50+ domains. Multiple campaigns. This is where agencies like us operate.

Start sending. Upgrade later.

 Tip 1: Bring it into your regular workflow                   
                                         
 When you're assigned a task:                          
 - Use Wispr Flow to fully explain what you're about to do           
 - Paste that into Cursor's plan mode                      
 - While it's generating, start working on the task manually          
 - When Cursor pings you with the plan, read through it             
 - Let it execute                                
                                         
 The reason you work manually while waiting: you have to get the task done   
 anyway. Might as well see how Cursor approaches it too.            
                                         
 Tip 2: Start with one-step workflows                      
                                         
 When you're first building, only create one or two-step automations.      
                                         
 Give an input. Call one API. That's it.                    
                                         
 Don't try to build something complicated on day one.              
                                         
 Tip 3: Let agents read the docs for you                    
                                         
 My team didn't want to sift through API documentation.             
                                         
 So we spin up agents whose entire context window is just reading the API docs 
 for Smartlead or whatever tool they're using.                 
                                         
 The agent learns it. Then it builds the automation.              
                                         
 Tip 4: Start by doing something simple like changing emojis                        
                                         
 We have an internal app. Everyone's first task is literally just changing   
 emojis in the UI to get comfortable with the workflow.             
                                         
 Tip 5: Screenshot your errors                         
                                         
 Every time I hit a problem, I screenshot it and paste it back into Claude   
 Code.                                     
                                         
 "Hey, why am I seeing this? How do I fix it?"                 
                                         
 It always fixes it.                              
                                         
 If you're reluctant to start, these are just some ways to ease in.

content:
I have to admit, six months ago I didn't get the point of MCPs.         
                                         
This post is for people who were like me. Also for my employees who are reluctant to start using these tools.                     
                                         
What is an MCP (Model Context Protocol)?                    
                                         
Think of it as a gateway for an AI agent to understand a tool.         
                                         
Instead of asking an agent to read API documentation (it will miss things),  
you connect it to an MCP. The agent figures out:                
 - What endpoints exist                             
 - What payloads to send                            
 - How to actually accomplish your task                     
                                         
Then you ask it to write the TypeScript or Python to make those API calls   
directly.                                   
                                         
Way more efficient. Way fewer tokens.                     
                                         
 My biggest tip:                                
                                         
 We're not actually doing a lot of work with MCPs as in moving data or doing work with MCP.             
                                         
We use them so agents understand the API documentation better.         
                                         
The MCP helps the agent learn the tool. Then we have Claude write actual code that calls the APIs.                                
                                         
That's the workflow:   
                           
 1. Connect MCP                                 
 2. Agent learns the tool                            
 3. Agent writes the automation code                      
 4. You run the code directly                          
                                        
 If you've been confused about MCPs, hopefully this helps.

content:
For 3 years people scared me away from using images in cold emails.

"Images hurt deliverability."
"Images trigger spam filters."
"Images increase email size."

All true.

But here's the math nobody does.

Let's say plain text gets you 80% inbox placement and 1% reply rate on 10,000 emails.

80% x 10,000 x 1% = 80 replies.

Now let's say adding an image drops inbox placement to 70%. But the image — a screenshot, a chart, a personalized mockup — increases reply rate to 1.8% among people who see it.

70% x 10,000 x 1.8% = 126 replies.

That's 57% more replies with WORSE deliverability.

The deliverability crowd will tell you the first scenario is better because your domain health stays cleaner long-term. And they're right. Probably. Maybe.

But the revenue crowd will tell you 126 replies beats 80 replies every day of the week. And they're also right.

Here's where I've seen images work:

1. Screenshots of the prospect's website with a specific callout
2. A before/after chart relevant to their industry
3. A Loom thumbnail (not embedded video, just the preview image with a play button)
4. A simple product screenshot that answers "what does this actually look like"

Here's where images don't work:

1. Stock photos
2. Marketing banners
3. Your company logo
4. Anything that looks like a newsletter

The real answer, like everything in cold email: test it.

Run 5,000 with the image. Run 5,000 without. Measure replies, not inbox placement.

Worse deliverability x higher conversion can absolutely beat perfect deliverability x mediocre conversion.

content:
Here's an email that broke all the rules and outperformed two years of testing.

We had a campaign we'd been split testing for two years across multiple clients in the same industry. We thought we had nailed the playbook. Tens of iterations of very similar things, and we had found the thing that was performing the best.

A new customer in the same industry joined and said, "Yeah, I know you're running that for other people, but I have my email that I think would work better."

We said, "Hey, we should split test this because we've been running this for a really long time. Show us your email."

He sent us an email that was five paragraphs long. Not five short paragraphs with one sentence each. Literally three to four sentences per paragraph.

I like to joke with him that he is sending love letters to these companies.

When we sent it, it absolutely blew our test out of the water.

Here's why I think it worked. He's competing with much larger companies in his space. Those companies are sending stone-cold emails with no feeling in them. 

His email, every single sentence was different. It felt like a real person who genuinely cared about the problem.

I think David Ogilvy once said that your first line sells the second line and your second line sells the third line.

When we say in cold email that every email should be under 100 words, it's not so much because it must. It's because we have nothing better to say.

His email had something better to say in every sentence.

Even "gurus" like me that are trying to share best practices — anything that you come up with as a test is probably always worth testing if it's easily reversible.

What's the most surprising test result you've ever seen?

I split tested multiple APIs to find recent company news, case studies, and the most recent blog article of a company and these were my favorite ones. 

During the snow storm, I couldn't resist the urge to figure out what everyone thinks about in a snow storm. 

"Which API should I use to find company news with the best rate limit, cost, and of course quality."

I tried 10 different tools and OpenWeb Ninja Real Time Web Search and Parallel Web Systems were my favorites. 

They each did something a little bit different which will help me pick what I want in the future. 

I manually researched 20 companies and their recent news, case studies, and blog to capture what the answers were and then did a bake off. 

OpenWeb Ninja was 10x cheaper than Parallel and super fast

Parallel caught far more of my signals but of course was more expensive and had some overly enthusiastic false positives.

So if I really need the company news to be super accurate for my list, I'd use Parallel. 

If I'm doing some really wide scraping and I needed something cheap that could get me Google SERP results, I'd go with OpenWeb Ninja.

content:
This workflow I made with Cursor and hosted on Railway saves me 6 hours a week on email deliverability tasks and our customers get much more consistent results from it. 

Over the last 6 months, we really systematized our email deliverability infrastructure. 

No more guessing and then ordering domains that we thought felt right. I built an SOP for everyone that I can give away at the end of the post. 

We would miss customers. Over order for some, under order for others. It was crazy. 

So we got extremely scientific about it. 

We keep all domains marked as status, Active, Insurance, or Cancel in Supabase. 

We always want to keep AT LEAST 50% of our Active daily sending volume in Insurance so that we can always rotate our domains. 

Every Friday, I would use a python script that would get the reply rates of all the domains in our campaigns so I could make decisions of what should be cancelled and what should be rotated from Insurance to Active. 

Once I had the numbers, spreadsheet warfare would begin. 

Making sure that every customer had enough and we didn't cancel too many domains. Numbers wouldn't look right so I'd check them manually. It was a mess.

Now, every Friday, I run this little Preview Global Rebatch and it send me a slack message with every customer, their daily send goal, how many domains are active, how many domains do we suggest to cancel, how many domains I need to buy more of, etc. 

And I hit accept and not only does it change all the statuses in our Supabase, it also pulls all of our customer's campaigns and swaps out the old domains for new domains. 

Easily my favorite workflow for deliverability. 

If you want our email deliverability SOP that goes over how we do this and how we work with Hypertide.io and Zapmail.ai to get it done, comment "primary" and I'll comment it back to you!

My team and I spent 9 hours talking through every customer we've ever worked with at Growth Engine X, what didn't work, and what worked the most often. 

I wanted to train my account managers to have historical knowledge of what we've done for customers.

The good, the bad, and the ugly. And so that we can take the transcript for some context training as well. 

As we went customer by customer, for every customer we had that we built a crazy outbound workflow that took screenshots of pricing pages and analyzed them to send a custom email, maybe 4-5 other customers would pop up and I'd say,

"Yeah, this was another one that we split test a ton of signals and value propositions and the best campaign was to basically help them imagine what it would be like to work with our customer."

No jiu jitsu workflows and multi table Clay builds. Really it was getting the content of the linkedin profile and the website. Structuring it and letting AI help write parts of the email to help the prospect understand how we could help in their situation. 

We generally would break it down into 2 frameworks of campaigns.

- A Creative ideas campaign - this is something I've posted about a ton but is basically where we send over 3 ideas of how we can help a company and each idea is a different flavor of our customer's offer. Still the best performing campaign for a number of our customers right now. 

Including 3 that are publicly traded companies. 

- An AI specificity campaign - Similar idea but instead of accidentally bloating the campaign with 3 bullet points, we opt for just a singular sentence. 

One of our customer's Donut thought they had everything dialed in before working with us (which they really almost did) and this one line tripled their response rates. 

So when doing your testing, triggers, workflows, awesome complicated emails are great. but don't forget to try plain straight to the point emails and AI emails that don't need anything other than a short company description to power them.

content:
Here are the 5 types of list building that come up in our agency and the tools we use to build them so hopefully you can get some ideas for your own niche lists. 

We get a lot of different list requests and even though they all sound different and have mini requests, I believe they can all be built in these 5 buckets. 

1) Standard Industry and Contact Filtering

Great when your target market has a great presence on LinkedIn or Google Maps and they self report their industries well. Still requires some keyword clean up and AI Fit scoring but 80% of people's lists can be accomplished this way. 

Prospeo.io recently released their database and is our daily driver for this because of their API. I now have a prospeo skill that I use that just queries whatever I want and helps me improve my searches. We can get the whole search and store it in supabase for usage later. 

2) Lookalikes

When standard filtering isn't going to be quite good enough and your customers are all within a niche. For instance, finding a list of fintech companies is a great use case to use a lookalike tool. 

Ocean.io and DiscoLike are the go-tos here. 

Discolike's recent case study on how Anthropic uses their tool was very compelling. 

3) Google Maps Scraping 

Great for local businesses or other companies that don't have a huge LinkedIn presence.

content:
In 2025, we launched 1,517 campaigns and generated over 60k positive responses across all of our customers. Here's 9 things we learned from the data. 

We had an AI analyze the offer, the leads in the campaign, and we made an AI summary. 

I threw 30 Claude sub agents at the database to answer a bunch of questions and here's what we learned. 

1. Our success metrics and average success of a campaign looks way different than it was 3 years ago. 

3 years ago, I said a campaign was successful and should be scaled if it was getting 1 positive response for every 300 people you reach out to. 

The numbers have moved for sure. I asked Claude to put our email response into quintiles and the results are in the screenshot. 

2. 70-90 words was optimal for email length

3. 2 Steps in an email sequence is ideal. 3 is ok. Anything over 3, HUGE reply drop off

4. For subject lines, including first name correlated with higher reply rates. I think this goes against 💜 🔮 Will Allred's data so I publish this at my peril. 

5. Monday - Thursday BEST reply days. Claude was saying we shouldn't even send on Fridays. Not sure we will make that leap but might be a good tip for those of you with a small market.

6. Heavy Spintax actually hurt some of our campaigns. It found lighter spintax did better. I think this has something to do with keeping control of the messaging with less variation

7. Industries that performed best for us - SaaS, Schools, Restaurants, E-commerce. This is for sure skewed by our data. We just have a lot of people targeting SaaS and then the people targeting Schools and Restaurants have crazy offers. 

8. Naming a case study actually hurt performance vs. just talking about outcomes. Definitely something I'm going to be keeping in mind. 

9. Generic AI personalization killed reply rates. 

I wanted to dig deeper into this one to see what it meant. We have naming conventions for our custom variables that match some templates we have in Clay so after manually reviewing, I could eye ball it and know what it meant. 

The generic AI that killed our reply rates was this trite, "Hey Eric, I saw you help people send cold email and I had a question." type stuff. 

Half way through the year, Taylor Haren even told me he thinks those are garbage and we reviewed mid year and I agreed

This was the AI that it said was garbage too. Any custom variable that was not in our template library and some custom template ones all correlated with higher response rates. 

I still have all the data. If you could ask a question about the success or failure of our campaigns, what would you ask it? 

DISCLAIMER: this is based on our internal data and might be skewed because of the customers we work with one way or another. If you have a question of your own campaigns, I always recommend not listening to people like me and just doing your own testing.

content:
There's only 2 rules you need to follow to be able to save anywhere from 50%-90% on your OpenAI input tokens by using cached inputs. 

I made a post recently about how you could save on your OpenAI calls with cached inputs and I did some testing to make sure it works.

Jeff Barg explained to me that the integration in Clay with OpenAI is ready to do cached inputs. We were prompting wrong (and so is the Clay metaprompter). 

The 2 rules you need to follow to have the highest chance of hitting cached inputs is to 

1. Make sure your prompt is over ~1,024 tokens. You can just ask chatgpt how many tokens a prompt is and it'll tell you. This is nothing for most of our prompts. 

2. As much of your prompt needs to be the same from the beginning of the prompt to whenever you make a change. 

That's what the caching of the input is. They already computed the beginning of the prompt and stored it. They recognize that it's been computed before and pass that saving to you. 

We were messing it up with putting custom parts of the prompt in the second or third sentence. 

Put all that custom stuff at the end and you will have a really high chance of hitting cached inputs. 

It feels like a black box because the Clay API at the point of this post doesn't tell you if you used cached inputs but they'll add that in soon!

Check out this video to see my experiment and proof that it's working with these two rules. 

https://lnkd.in/eFgRrhVK

Easy CTA again hammering on the efficiency of the equipment. Not if they need something new.

content:
I've been completely wrong about AI prompting, and it's cost me thousands of dollars and it might be costing you money too. 

For months, I've been telling my team (and all of you) to structure prompts like this:

1. Tell the AI what you want it to do
2. Give it the data to analyze and reference
3. Provide examples of good outputs

I didn't realize that this approach wastes tokens. Especially when you're running outbound campaigns at scale.

I know this may seem obvious to technical people out there but I didn't even consider making a change. 

I had a call with my enterprise rep from OpenAI last week and they asked me why I wasn't using cached inputs based on my use case. 

I didn't even consider it because we use the Clay OpenAI integration.

Cached inputs save 50% on input tokens for GPT-4o mini, and 90% on GPT-4 when the input stays the same.

For those of us using AI for outbound messaging, this is exactly what we're doing. Running the same prompt structure over and over with different prospect data.

But the prompt needs to stay the same for as long as possible for the inputs to cache.

My old approach was mixing up the prompt by putting variable data (company descriptions, prospect info) in the middle.

The correct way:

Put everything that changes at the very bottom of your prompt.

Keep the instructions, examples, and framework identical at the top.

Only vary the prospect-specific data at the end.

I met with Jeff Barg on the Clay team directly about this and you shouldn't have to change all your integrations. The prompt will cache automatically with how they have the integration set up. 

This might seem obvious to technical people, but this is the ignorance debt you pay when you're not technical.

I'm sorry I made the wrong suggestion for so long.

If you're running AI-powered outbound campaigns and not using cached inputs correctly, you're burning money.

AI-only campaigns without images
Look-alike campaigns
New in roll campaigns

Everything in marketing is about testing, and so if it's worth sending the image, send the image.

content:
The tests are in and we are not allowing generic AI personalizations based on company descriptions as first lines anymore. I could prove this raised reply rates but recently, in most markets, it falls flat.

We try to always lead with some kind of signal or pain point that we research but if we can't do that, we would fall back to a company description based personalization. 

Something like, "I saw you help fitness coaches retain clients and I wanted to get connected."

We used to see increased reply rates when we personalized first lines with AI-generated content scraped from company websites.

Now the data is pointing the opposite direction.

Sophisticated buyers recognize generic AI personalization instantly which hurts your message:
- "Hey, I saw how you helped fitness enthusiasts breathe better..."
- "I noticed you're focused on helping local businesses..."
- Generic references to their company description

They've seen it a thousand times.

Here's what we do instead:

If we have a real signal: We use it. Something specific, custom-scraped, that ties directly to their problem and our value prop.

**If we don't have a signal:** We treat cold email like a banner ad.

Put the offer in the preview text.
Make it punchy.
No fake personalization.

Think about it: When someone's scrolling on their phone or web browser, they see the subject line + preview text together.

That's your click opportunity.

Stop wasting time generating first lines from company descriptions.

Unless you have custom research that goes well beyond what's publicly available on their homepage, foregoing AI personalization and writing punchy, split-tested first lines performs better.

We've seen this deteriorate over the past six months across our customer base and as someone that would suggest it based on the data, I want to correct the record and say we're out of it now.

Made this video explaining how you can use Cursor to scrape Google Maps and stop messing with custom coding it yourself. Here's the overall guideline to get this done below. 

Why Scrape Google Maps?

LinkedIn isn’t enough: Some businesses, especially local ones, lack a LinkedIn presence.

Google Maps is universal: Almost every legitimate business is listed here.

This method is ideal for local businesses or industries with limited LinkedIn activity.

Tools You'll Need:
Cursor: An AI-powered coding assistant and development environment.

Google Maps Extractor API:
RapidAPI version: Affordable and reliable.
Serper.dev, Outscraper, or similar APIs are also compatible.

CSV of ZIP codes or locations: Optional, but useful for targeted searching.

Clay or CRM: For storing and using your scraped data in email workflows.

Step-by-Step Instructions
1. Get Your API Access Set Up
Visit RapidAPI.com's Google Maps Extractor page (or your preferred API provider).

Subscribe to a suitable plan (e.g., $100/mo for 500,000 requests).

Copy your API key from the provider.

Note: One API request = 1 Google Maps page of results.

2. Open Cursor and Start a Project

Launch Cursor and create a new workspace.
Use natural language prompts like:
"Help me set up a workflow to search Google Maps for businesses in a CSV of ZIP codes. Use the RapidAPI Google Maps Extractor endpoint."
Cursor will write the necessary code for you (this might be Python, JavaScript, etc.).

3. Teach Cursor the API Endpoint
In Cursor, paste in the API documentation from RapidAPI (e.g., the search or locate endpoint).

Show it the input parameters and expected response format.

This improves Cursor’s ability to generate valid code.

4. Build Your Scraping Workflow
Provide prompts like:
"Loop through this list of ZIP codes, perform a Google Maps search for 'restaurants', and save the business name, address, category, and phone number to a CSV."

Modify as needed: e.g., "Go 3–5 pages deep" or "also fetch review data".

Let Cursor adjust the code and test locally within the tool.

5. Once you’ve scraped your data:

Export it into a clean CSV.
Import it into Clay to find owner email and contact information.

Here's how we use Cursor to know which domains are healthy vs. unhealthy and remove them automatically and replace them live in our campaigns.

Most people wait until their cold email campaigns tank to check deliverability. By then, it's too late.

We built an automated health scoring system that flags problems before they kill reply rates.

Here's how it works:

The Smartlead API pulls our metrics:
- Sends last 2 weeks
- Sends last week  
- Sends this week
- Reply rate last 2 weeks
- Reply rate last week
- Reply rate this week

Cursor uses Python to:
- Compare reply rates to our baseline
- Flag domains as "suggested cancel" if they're consistently underperforming
- Flag "warning" when reply rate drops sharply week-over-week

Then we have a human review checkpoint.

Once approved, Cursor updates Supabase with domain status:
- Active (healthy and running)
- Insurance (backup domains ready to swap in)
- Canceled (removed from rotation)

The insurance logic is key:

We keep at least 50% of our active volume in insurance domains. Goal is 100%.

Cursor even suggests how many inboxes to buy based on current health trends.

The outcome: fully automated health scoring with team-wide visibility in Supabase.

No more guessing which domains are working. No more manual spreadsheet hell.

We see the health of every domain in real-time and act before campaigns suffer.

When targeting Enterprise companies with automated outbound, this playbook has been our go to for over 2 years and still performs to this day. This is the line we make in Clay. 

Hey {{first_name}} - reaching out because your profile says {{custom reason based on their profile and your solution}}. Should I be reaching out to {{other team member in same department 1}} or {{other team member in same department 2}} instead? 

I love it for multiple reasons.

1) makes a great "break up email"
2) adds in that same thing you would normally do if you were manually writing the message and explaining why you picked them in the first place. 
3) If you're trying to target the marketing person that owns the website at an enterprise company, how on Earth would you ever distinguish which "Head of Marketing" is correct. 

This allows you to still send custom messaging (usually in follow up emails) to your prospects and usually 1 of 4 things happens.

1) They are the right person and they respond because they saw the extra care in the email.
2) They confirm that one of those 2 people are the right people.
3) They say "actually it's neither of them, reach out to this person"
4) They ignore you which was what they could have done anyway. 

Some things to keep in mind. If you run this for small companies, you can go outside their department. 

If you do this for large companies you should really stay within the same department and as much as you can name drop people in the same state to increase the odds that they know their names.

content:
This is what I wish I knew about bounce rates when I first started. When I first started, I thought all bounces happened because the email address didn't exist. 

But there are so many other reasons for bounce issues and all can help you understand if email deliverability is a problem for your campaigns. 

1) Erol Toker and I talk about this all the time that people marking your email as spam is by far the worst thing for your sender reputation. Repeated bounces is second worst BUT Erol and I in different experiments purposely bounced a ton of emails and landed in inbox the next day. 

So still goes to show that getting marked as spam is by far the worst. 

2) Bounces happen from hard bounces and soft bounces. Hard bounces are those bounces where the email is incorrect. Soft bounces can happen for a number of reasons. But if you see status code 550, that means your inboxes are being flagged as spam and the recipients aren't letting it come through (even to land in spam). 

3) another reason you could be getting bounces (that can get up to literally 100%) is if you're sending from outlook and they throttle your sending because they think as an email sender that you're sending spam. 

So in your email sending platform like Instantly or Smartlead, the bounces will sky rocket which is why you want to keep the sender bounce protection and domain threshold rate limit turned on to avoid this. 

Bounces aren't just incorrect emails, they help you know which domains are fried and which are still healthy.

1) score their Do not contact list (their customer list) for all industries that their customers self report that they are in. 

Use AI to also analyze the company descriptions that keep coming up to make a list of good keyword fits as well. 

2) Put any industry filter that a company self selected as their linkedin company industry as one search. 

Another search that uses the keyword matching in case that's broad enough. 

Another search with the Clay AI sub industry and derived data filters. 

3) Manually review which looks the best that is broad enough but still high quality. 

4) Using the best list source, clean the companies with Open Router OSS 20B model (1/3rd price of 4o mini for the intelligence of o3-mini). 

Filter for a company TAM that we can then find contacts from. 

The AI needs some back and forth for sure and to make the AI prompt, we use the Clay sourced data to manually find good fits and bad fits and use those examples in a ChatGPT window that can create the Openrouter json request for us. 

That way we can try to capture as much TAM as possible that is still qualified with an AI that has reasoning capabilities.

content:
Last week, I explained to the Sell Better audience that I think AI generated emails fit into 4 tiers. Use these buckets to brainstorm how it could apply to your business. 

We all want the perfect AI generated email but not every offer is capable of getting the best email. 

Top Tier - the famous Jordan Crawford Permissionless Value Prop email. An email so good, they would pay to receive it. Using your own internal data, data you scrape publicly, and AI to make a message that shows you did your research, uncovered a problem, and gave them a taste of the solution, while explaining how you can help more in the future. 

Second Tier - an email based on what you would research about a company for 10 minutes manually and using AI to change your messaging based on that. 

Not as in depth as Jordan's best following similar principles. Think about what you were to research manually about someone, keep track of what sources you check, and how it helps you make decisions on what to say. 

Use the literal messages you sent manually as the training data for your AI. 

Third Tier - Using AI to help someone imagine what it would be like if you were to work together. Simple, but still wildly effective. Basically a liner adding specificity about what you do and how it could specifically help them. 

Fourth Tier - Attention Hacking. Bottom of the barrel you probably stole it from someone on LinkedIn but everyone has to put food on the table so I get it. Especially in industries that don't receive very many sophisticated emails, these can still work. 

We've seen emailing local businesses and name dropping the top steakhouse in the area still increases replies over not doing it. 

So when making AI outbound workflows in Clay or other places. 

First think - is there anything I can send them that's inherently valuable and custom to their business without having to speak to them that I can automate. 

Second - what would I say if I were reaching out manually anyway?

Third - use AI to make the email more specific to their situation and business from information you can easily find on their website. 

Fourth - do what you gotta do haha

Any other ideas for tiers?

content:
This is how can are trying to make landing in the inbox inevitable for our customers at Growth Engine X.

Some first principles that guide me in this process decision making. 

1) no matter how good your campaign is, people are going to mark you as spam and keeping back up infrastructure is necessary. 

2) Some providers like proofpoint and outlook can't be beat with just 2 weeks of warmup. Longer warmup times for these inboxes are necessary. 

3) We need to be catching bad domains as they happen so that we can cycle in our back up infrastructure, cancel those bad domains, and reorder new ones to keep a healthy stack of domains. 

What we do about each below.

Every customer that joins us gets an infrastructure that can send 5,000 emails per day off the bat. Most of our customers start by sending 500-1500 emails per day. Setting up more than necessary from the beginning allows us to 

- Scale volume immediately if a successful campaign is found
- Always have back up infrastructure in case the first batch of inboxes goes wrong. 
- Allow for inboxes to reach a 4 week warming to have a higher chance of breaking into Outlook/Proofpoint inboxes. Some inboxes even get 2 months of warming before we ever use them. 

This investment early on allows us to be prepared for 1 and 2. 

If a customer does ramp up to 5,000 a day, we buy another batch of inboxes capable of sending 2,500 emails per day and start that warmup. 

Hypertide.io is our main partner here.

We leverage the Smartlead API and Supabase to catch bad domains. 

Every Friday, we pull a report of the last 3 weeks of sending per domain. The bottom 10% of domains based on reply rate are cancelled and reordered with fresh domains from Hypertide. 

If we think a customer is having more deliverability issues than just the bottom 10% of domains, we will go even further. 

Basically, investing early, keeping inboxes in reserve, and weekly reply rate monitoring are some recent things we have implemented to try to stay ahead of deliverability issues. 

And because Hypertide makes it so easy to order inboxes, anyone of any size can follow this with an automated system or just a weekly manual report.

content:
One niche tip we’ve found for Claygent: tell it not to use its full capabilities.

Claygent works broadly by creating a Google search, finding links, then visiting websites to complete tasks. Normally that’s great, but sometimes it stops too early or gets distracted on the wrong page.

We found that if you tell it not to go to the website and just keep researching via Google searches, results are actually better.

Why? Google has already built the most powerful scraper in the world. Claygent tapping into it gives you clean, surface-level data fast.

Example: A customer asked us to find school contacts (Principal, Superintendent, Athletic Director, etc.). 

If Claygent goes on the site, it might grab just the Principal and stop. But if you force it to stay on Google and try multiple search operators, it surfaces many more of them.

Tip: Use ChatGPT or Metaprompter to help you build prompts with multiple Google search operators baked in.

This method is especially useful for finding contacts that don’t have LinkedIn profiles, schools are a perfect use case.

content:
3 things we have changed in our Email Deliverability workflow at Growth Engine X and 2 things we are keeping the same that I think everyone should think about doing. 

1) Cleaning up bad domains with Smartlead API and reordering on Hypertide.io

Smartlead upgraded their API. Now we can get the exact reply rate statistics on a domain level for any time period that we want. 

We're sending this data to Supabase and then writing SQL queries to figure out which domains we should be canceling and which domains we should be keeping. 

2) Sending to Google first and then harder to reach inboxes when campaigns are falling flat. Leadmagic just made a tool called inboxriskscore(.)com you can use to identify easy vs. hard domains to send emails to. 

We've also been seeing that Outlook/Proof Point is harder to break into. Nick Abraham released a report that 10% of his replies at his agency are coming from Outlook. 

The only thing that we've seen consistently combat these low inbox placements on these harder-to-reach inboxes is letting the domains age for a longer time.

 But customers can't usually wait for 4-8 weeks to start an email campaign.

Start with a regular 2-week warmup, sending to Google inboxes, and then start bringing in the Outlook proof point inboxes if necessary. 

3) Auto batching inboxes into campaigns to keep within domain rate limit threshold. Smartlead implemented a domain rate limit threshold to protect Azure sending accounts but it messed up our sending volume. 

We easily use Cursor now to plug into our Supabase to find relevant accounts and divide them appropriately across campaigns so that ever hypertide domain is dedicated to one campaign and one campaign only. 

Things that are staying the same. 

1) Continue to keep open tracking off. Cancelling open tracking test and moving to just reply tracking. 

I'm still not completely against open tracking, but for the past four to six weeks that we've been trying the experiment, we saw positive responses go down on the days that we were tracking opens, and reply rate was just as good of a metric to be watching. 

So we'll cancel using this test as a systemic thing that we automatically do every week and only turn it on as needed. 

2) Buying capacity with Hypertide to send 5,000 emails per day even if a client needs 1,000 per day just to make sure we always have reserve and they age much longer. 

Still keeping 50% of sending capacity in warming reserve at full volume.

Always keep more than you need in reserve so you can try as best as possible to not get caught with no warmed up healthy inboxes. 

Anything you're trying lately that you would add?

content:
Here’s how to dynamically change the case study in your outbound emails, without burning OpenAI tokens.

Mentioning the right case study for the right type of company (CPG with 100 employees vs SaaS with 700) is a no-brainer addition to your campaigns. 

I just saw someone uploading all of their case studies to Google Gemini Flash 2.5 (which was a good idea since it does well on the needle in the haystack benchmark). 

But it's still rolling the dice in my opinion and if you have a lot of case studies, it might not output precisely what you want. 

I'd rather use if/then statements to lookup and find the one I want to make my messaging. 

How we do it in Clay:

1. Enrich case studies: Get domain, company name, industry, headcount, and add the sentence you want to output if there’s a match.

 1A. Generate an AI column of keywords so you can distinguish between “retail apparel” vs “retail electronics.”

2. Upload to Clay in the same workbook as your workflow.

3. Enrich your prospect list with the same parameters.

4. Create a lookup key like {{Industry}} :: {{Headcount Range}} for both tables.

5. Lookup multiple rows between tables. Use your custom keywords to break ties.

6. Filter overlaps with AI if needed to pick the best match.

Result: the right case study sentence appears in your outbound automatically without hallucinations or wasted tokens.

content:
After running millions of outbound emails, these are the patterns I see that kill meeting rates.

1. Using a calendar link as your CTA.

 Calendar links feel convenient, but security filters + human behavior both work against them. People are more likely to reply “Sure, let’s chat” than click a random link. Earn the reply first, then offer booking options.

2. Not following up fast enough.

 Speed is leverage. The longer you wait, the colder the lead gets. Reply the same day if you can — it signals you’re paying attention.

3. Not following up enough.

 There’s a balance: don’t spam, but if someone raised their hand once, don’t stop until they book or say no. I positively responded to Rippling and it took that poor soul 8 follow ups for me to book. I'm still sorry but it wasn't my biggest priority. 

4. Not adding value in follow-ups.

 Repeating “just checking in” is lazy. Each touch should reinforce why the call matters: ROI, risk avoidance, case study, new idea. After a few tries, you can even add a kicker (we’ve seen success offering a gift card to qualified prospects at this stage).

5. Not giving booking options.

 Don’t force a link or a back-and-forth. Do both.
 “Would Tuesday at 9am ET or Thursday at 2pm ET work? Or if it’s easier, here’s my calendar.”

 You’re reducing friction while respecting preferences. Some people like booking with a calendly, others are offended by it. I don't get it but appease both people. 

6. Not following up across channels.

 A reply rate isn’t the same as a meeting rate. Sometimes an extra LinkedIn DM or quick phone call takes a warm response over the finish line. People book with people, not just with inboxes.

Just a couple of things we've seen make a difference that are obvious but sometimes we needed to be reminded more than we need to learn.

Steps to running the WORST outbound campaign in history:

Don’t validate any of your leads.

For that matter, don’t use any filters, just target all CEOs.

Write an email that’s 12 sentences long talking in depth about how your features are the best.

Only ask to book a call while providing no explanation on why that call would be worthwhile to them.

Don’t even try to send their first name and get it wrong purposely. Call everyone in the campaign “Jives.”

Send from Mailchimp in HTML format.

Ask everyone to book on a calendar link.

Add a request for payment in bitcoin to make the spam filters happy.

Send from a domain you purchased an hour before launch.

Send 3 emails to them in one day and follow up every day for the next 7 days.

While this is kind of funny to think about, it also helps people remember the best practices when we try to think about how we can do worse at something.

Charlie Munger called this inversion thinking and is a frame I think about when campaigns aren't going our way and I I'm troubleshooting why.

content:
As Clay's largest user, we've learned a ton about scaling with the platform.
Here are the 5 lessons I talked about on stage at Sculpt in San Francisco recently. (Link to video at the end). 

Clay Rules & Best Practices

1. Always Always Always Use Conditional Formulas on Paid Integrations.

Seems super simple and obvious but getting your team in this habit helps to prevent unnecessary API calls and only trigger paid integrations when data truly needs enrichment.


2. Save Paid Data Externally

Store enriched data in CRM or Supabase, not inside Clay only.
I pay $30 a month for Supabase and just one of our databases amongst over 20 has 11.4M records.

3. Leverage Scheduled Sources

Automate evergreen campaigns that continuously refresh and send new leads into workflows without manual input. This features is still under used by people that have cracked an outbound campaign for themselves and need to keep it on all the time without forgetting. 

4. The formula generator can really do a lot. If you want the same thing to happen every time it sees an input, try this before using AI. 

Use formulas for:

Cleaning and combining data
If/Then logic
Lead scoring
State abbreviation

Reminder: Clay formulas run on JavaScript, so almost any data transformation is possible.

5. The GEX AI Prompting Framework

Prompting Rules

The 10-Minute Manual Research Rule:
Don't steal other people's playbooks. Think about when you are manually researching a company. What are you looking for if you had 10 minutes to research them? And how does that change your message? 

One Thing at a Time:
Give AI a single, focused task, avoid multitasking prompts.

Safeguards:
Build filters for low-context outputs (e.g., return “purple” when uncertain).

Use Examples:
 Always include examples in prompts for better accuracy.

Meta Prompting:
 Ask ChatGPT “What questions do you have to improve this prompt?” before finalizing.

Reasoning First:
 For high-stakes tasks (like industry classification), ask AI to output reasoning before its final answer.

Handle Edge Cases:
 Be ready to prompt around specific constraints (e.g., tone, banned words, output format, length).

Mindset Takeaway
“AI is the smartest thing in the world built to solve Calculus problems.
 I promise it can write your emails, you just need to give it some TLC.”

Overall: 
 → Think like a system designer, not a button clicker.
 → Use Clay, Supabase, and AI together to build repeatable, data-rich workflows that scale outbound.

content:
Unpopular opinion: the best outbound campaigns that we have seen usually work right away. If they don’t, something needs to change drastically. Here’s what we look at first in all cases:

1. Is our list as correct as we thought it was?

 We do a lot of checks internally: inclusion/exclusion keywords, AI checks, job title matching. Did something slip through the cracks?

2. Is our list correct but our decision to target them with this messaging wrong?

 We talk to our customer and use ChatGPT for deeper analysis. We even look at open job postings to understand what roles are being asked to do.

3. How can we change the messaging of what’s in it for the prospect?

 The overarching value prop isn’t always the best outbound message. Break down individual features and test what resonates.

For example, Clay’s main value prop is connecting to 150+ integrations. That doesn’t resonate in outbound. The best campaign we ran focused on name-dropping customer case studies and showing how to find more companies like them automatically.

4. Are there other buying signals we can add?

 Signals reduce list size and add complexity but they sharpen targeting. Think: what would we research for 10 minutes if we were reaching out manually, and how does it change the message?

5. Have we tried lookalike campaigns?

 They add two benefits:

Messaging comes directly from a case study, so it’s less hypothesis and more storytelling.

Prospects always react better when they know something has already worked for a peer.

From there, it comes down to the biggest insight from Facebook ads: the companies making the most money were doing the most split testing.

Different channel, same principle, keep split testing between lists, messaging, and lead magnets until you find what works.

content:
There are 2 reasons to hire an outbound agency. If you don’t know which one you are, that’s where problems occur.

Reason 1: To learn about the channel faster and experiment with new ideas. You want to get started quickly, tap into expertise, and have someone take care of everything while you learn.

Reason 2: You already have something working and want to scale. An agency can give you better economies of scale, automation, error fixes, time savings, and insights from the broader market.

Every company at one point needs to learn about the channel whether they use an agency or not — but not every company is ready to scale it.

The biggest problem in agency relationships? Customers not understanding what they’re paying for if they’ve never done outbound or marketing before. (Founder-led sales transitions are often the scariest).

If you haven’t run campaigns before and think “This company is just going to fix our pipeline issues,” maybe they will, maybe they won’t. You might not know your ICP as well as you think, or you might not have communicated your messaging clearly enough.

If you’re looking to work with any agency and you don’t have the learning mindset first, the relationship could be doomed from the beginning.

I was asked by one of those fancy four-letter-domain tech companies: “What are other people using AI for in outbound?”

Here’s a better question:

 👉 What is your team manually doing in 10 minutes of research on a prospect, and how does that change your messaging?

Here are some AI workflows we’ve built for other companies:

Using Serper to pull Google Maps reviews and adjust messaging based on good/bad reviews.

Using Screenshot(dot)net + Bannerbear to send personalized screenshots of a company’s sustainability page.

Analyzing if a company has employees overseas and adjusting messaging accordingly.

Pulling pricing/plans pages to create product video ideas.

Clicking through a site with Browserbase to see if retail products have insurance protections.

And that’s just a handful.

If your workflows can be copied easily by someone who isn’t your competitor, they’re not deep enough to be valuable in outbound.

Think: what would you research manually about a company in 10 minutes? Then automate that.

content:
After running outbound campaigns as a service for 4 years now, most of the glitter of new tech is gone for me and we keep coming back to the same principles.

In order to get a positive response in cold email you need 3 things.

An infrastructure to send emails from, a list to send emails to, and a message to send them.

If you’re starting your first outbound campaign, here’s how I’d get set up quickly for myself.

For inbox infrastructure, this is a solved problem. Get an Instantly or Smartlead account and either get inboxes set up through them or go to Zapmail / Hypertide. (Be on the lookout for .co domain sales as that can help save a ton of money).

For the list of companies to send to, get yourself a simple B2B database or Clay account to pull lists. If the platform gives email addresses, make sure to validate them and use a third party software to find more emails.

Leadmagic is the fastest provider in our waterfall so they are first but we also use Prospeo, Get Prospect, IcyPeas, and TryKitt to find and validate emails.

When it comes to making a base level message, personally, I love giving ChatGPT a ton of context about what I’m doing and then asking it what Josh Braun would say in an email. Use the transcribe feature to talk back and forth with the copy for fast editing. 

Add some extra spice and use Clay to try to replicate the workflow you do manually when you research a company for 10 minutes and how it changes your message.

From there, you are about 80% of the way to a campaign that many professional agencies would set up for you.

If you have more questions, I wrote a 112-page doc on how we think about doing this that I’ll link in the comments. You can upload it to your favorite LLM and ask questions about it.

content:
One way we closed 6 deals in 3 months with 90 minutes of work was to use cold email to expand traditionally inbound channels. Here’s our playbook. 

Admittedly, I’m not the biggest fan of talking to dead cold prospects for our offerings.

Too many people are sending the same “I’m so desperate we will work for free until we get results” kind of message that changes the expectations for prospects when they talk to us and they expect everything to be free. 

I thought, “If we could just get more people into watching my YouTube (where our best customers come from) I could warm them up there and then they’ll reach out when ready.”

So the question is, how do we get a dead cold prospect to see my YouTube. 

It starts with what does everyone who would be serious customers want? 

They could want a number of things, but our best customers want some kind of signal to know they should be reaching out. 

By far the broadest and most useful signal for any b2b company is knowing when a new department leader joins a new company or gets a promotion.
 
So we made a list with Clay of every person new in their role in the past 30 days and included their job title, industry, company headcount, etc. so we could send an email that looked like. 

"Hey, our customers love to target people new in their role. Here’s a list of all of the new people in the United States with a director and above position. I also included the company industry, headcount, description, and state so you could filter for what you want. Just request access to the list so that I know you got it."

Then anyone that would request access to the list we would follow up saying “Hey we actually give this list away every other Monday. Want to be added to the newsletter so you always get this list?”

4/5 people say yes to this in which we add them to the newsletter and send the list as well as sending one of my YouTube videos to get them into our content. 

We used beehiiv to keep the newsletter pumping and of course Clay to get the new hire data on repeat. 

If you have the ability to wait for really great leads to warm themselves up in your other channels, using outbound to get them there can be a great way to leverage cold email.

content:
Whenever I post about the average reply rate that we see, agency owners I'm close with message me and tell me to stop because their customers then ask about getting that average reply. But often people are asking the wrong question. 

We get asked all the time, "What's a response rate that we can expect?"

The real answer is: If you were to take all of our customers and divide the amount of positive responses we get by how many emails we have to send out, the number right now is about 1 positive response out of 425 contacts that we enroll. (Up from 1 in 300 2 years ago I might add). 

But there's so much nuance underneath this. We have some people that get one positive response for every 78 people that they reach out to. 

Their LTV is $2,000.

Another customer, (who has happily worked with us for a year I might add) gets 1 positive response for every 2,000 leads.

Their LTV is $200k

 Asking what the average is fine, so that you can have an expectation of performance. But you also need to consider:

How many experiments have you run?
Have you truly thought through a lot of ideas and tested them?
How many times have you changed your copywriting and framing?

As long as you're constantly experimenting and trying new things, your response rate eventually is just what your response rate is in your market. And you have to make sure that that math works out for your business in particular.

On open tracking, it's just so powerful to be able to know exactly which inboxes are having issues. We've started turning it on every Thursday and Friday and removing low performing inboxes on Saturday with the Smartlead API.
